questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Counting the three components a compound selector contributes
questions.learningObjective: count the identifier, class and type components of a compound selector in order
questions.stem: A stylesheet holds `#main .card a { color: black }` and `#main p.em span { color: teal }`. The specificity of a selector is a triple of counts: identifiers first, then classes and attribute and pseudo-class selectors, then type selectors and pseudo-elements. Give the triple each of the two selectors resolves to, in that order, and say which of the two wins on an anchor that sits inside an emphasised paragraph inside a card whose main ancestor carries the identifier.

options.text: One, one, one and one, one, two, so the second selector wins because the type count is higher
One, one, one and one, one, one, so the two selectors tie and source order alone decides
options.misconception: believes the last type selector in a compound is not counted

options.text: Three, three, three and three, three, three, so the second selector wins because it names more parts
options.misconception: believes every simple selector in a compound counts in the same component

options.text: One, one, one and one, one, two, so the first selector wins because identifiers outrank everything else
options.misconception: believes one identifier outweighs any number of type selectors

questions.explanation: The three components are counted in separate columns and compared left to right, so a difference in the first column decides the contest before the second is consulted. In the first selector there is one identifier, one class and one type selector, giving one, one, one. In the second there is one identifier, one class and two type selectors, the paragraph and the span, giving one, one, two. The two triples agree in the first two columns, so the comparison falls through to the third, where two beats one, and the second selector wins. That ordering is why the first selector does not win merely because it contains an identifier: the identifier comparison already succeeded on a tie, and only then does the next column matter. The rule to carry away is that a column is only consulted when the columns to its left are equal, which is what makes a single identifier stronger than any number of class selectors and a class selector stronger than any number of type selectors.
questions.hint: Count the three columns separately, then compare the columns from the left and stop at the first that differs.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: What each part of a selector list is scored on
questions.learningObjective: trace the winner for one element that matches two parts of the same selector list
questions.practice: tracing a selector list across two rules
questions.stem: A stylesheet holds `.big { color: gray }` and then `h1, #lead { color: teal }`. The document has one heading that carries the class and no identifier, and one heading that carries both the class and the identifier. A cascade resolver is run against each, printing the winning colour and the selector that produced it. What does it print?

options.text: Teal for both, because a selector list takes the score of its most specific part
options.misconception: believes a list behaves like the matching function that also takes the strongest part

options.text: Teal for the first heading and teal for the second, because the rule with a list always wins over a rule with one selector
options.misconception: believes the number of selectors in a rule decides the winner

options.text: Gray for the first heading and gray for the second, because the class rule comes from the more specific selector in each case
options.misconception: believes the earlier rule wins whenever a list is present

options.text: Gray from the class for the first heading, and teal from the identifier for the second, because each part of a list carries its own score

questions.explanation: A selector list is a convenience, not a unit. Each part is matched against the element independently and carries its own score, and the part that actually matched is the part whose score is compared. For the first heading the only part of the list that matches is the type selector, whose score of zero, zero, one loses to the class rule's zero, one, zero, so the class rule wins and the heading is gray. For the second heading both parts match, and the identifier scores one, zero, zero, which beats the class on the very first column, so the list wins and the heading is teal. The second option is the trap, because it is a true statement about a different construct: the matching function that takes the strongest of its arguments is a separate rule, and assuming a plain list behaves that way makes every list look stronger than it is. The practical consequence is that a list cannot be strengthened or weakened as a whole, so splitting a selector into a list to make it win is a way of doing nothing.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the list actually matches each element, and score only that part.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: The score a matching function takes from the argument that matched
questions.learningObjective: compute the specificity a functional pseudo-class inherits from its most specific argument
questions.practice: computing specificity inside a matching function
questions.stem: A resolver is asked for the specificity of five selectors: `:is(#a, p)`, `:is(.a, p)`, `:is(p, span)`, `li:is(ul, .nav)` and `a:not(.x, #y)`. The rule is that the matching function scores as the most specific of its arguments, computed by comparing identifier count first, then class count, then type count. Give the triple for each of the five, in that order.

options.text: Zero, zero, zero for all five, because a functional pseudo-class adds nothing of its own and the arguments are not counted
options.misconception: believes a matching function's arguments never reach the score

options.text: One, zero, zero then zero, one, zero then zero, zero, one then zero, one, one then one, zero, two
options.misconception: believes the exclusion function also adds a class of its own

options.text: One, zero, zero then zero, one, zero then zero, zero, one then zero, one, one then one, zero, one
Zero, zero, one then zero, one, zero then zero, zero, one then zero, one, one then one, one, one
options.misconception: believes a matching function scores as the first argument rather than the strongest

questions.explanation: A functional pseudo-class contributes no component of its own and instead adopts the score of the most specific argument in its list, which is what the first column of each triple shows. Comparing the first two arguments identifier-first means the identifier argument wins the first selector outright, giving one, zero, zero. In the second there is no identifier, so the class argument wins over the type argument and gives zero, one, zero. In the third only type arguments remain and both score the same, so the result is zero, zero, one. In the fourth the surrounding type selector contributes its own column and the class argument inside the function contributes another, giving zero, one, one. The fifth is the case that trips people up: the exclusion function follows the same rule as the matching one, so the identifier argument dominates even though it is being excluded, and the surrounding anchor adds its own type column, giving one, zero, one. The cost of this rule is that a broad-looking selector can be specific in disguise, so the arguments to these functions need the same discipline as a written-out selector.
questions.hint: Take the strongest argument by comparing identifier count first, then class count, then type count, and add whatever the rest of the selector contributes.

questions.topic: The score a zeroing function contributes
questions.learningObjective: compute the specificity a zeroing functional pseudo-class contributes
questions.practice: computing specificity inside a zeroing function
questions.stem: A resolver is asked for the specificity of six selectors: `:where(#a)`, `:where(.a)`, `:where(#a, .b, p)`, `p:where(#a)`, `:where(.a, .b)` and `#x:where(#y)`. One functional pseudo-class is specified to contribute nothing at all to the score, no matter what its arguments are, while the rest of the selector is counted normally. Give the triple for each of the six, in that order.

options.text: One, zero, zero then zero, one, zero then one, zero, zero then zero, zero, one then zero, one, zero then one, zero, zero
options.misconception: believes the zeroing function scores like the matching function

options.text: Zero, zero, zero then zero, zero, zero then zero, zero, zero then zero, zero, one then zero, zero, zero then one, zero, zero
Zero, zero, zero then zero, zero, zero then zero, zero, zero then zero, zero, one then zero, one, zero then one, one, zero
options.misconception: believes the zeroing function counts type arguments but not the rest

options.text: Zero, zero, zero then zero, zero, zero then zero, zero, zero then zero, zero, one then zero, zero, zero then zero, zero, zero
options.misconception: believes a zeroing function cancels the score of the whole selector

questions.explanation: The whole point of the zeroing function is that its arguments are ignored by the score, so the first, second, third and fifth selectors all come out as zero, zero, zero no matter how strong their arguments are. The two exceptions prove the rule, because in each of them something outside the function is being counted. The type selector in the fourth contributes one type column, giving zero, zero, one, and the identifier before the function in the sixth contributes one identifier column, giving one, zero, zero. The fourth option is the mistake this property is designed to prevent: the function does not cancel the selector, it only refuses to raise it, so a strong identifier elsewhere in the selector still counts. That asymmetry is exactly why the function exists. A rule that should apply to any element regardless of what the markup adds is written with it so the markup cannot outrank the rule, and the pattern for a design system's base rules is a list of zeroing functions around a bare type selector, which is the score that a single class in the markup can beat.
questions.hint: Count the parts of the selector that are outside the function, and ignore everything inside it.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: The score a relative selector inherits from its argument
questions.learningObjective: compute the specificity a relative-argument pseudo-class inherits
questions.practice: computing specificity inside a relative pseudo-class
questions.stem: A resolver is asked for the specificity of five selectors: `:has(.x)`, `:has(#y)`, `section:has(> .row)`, `li:has(+ li.more)` and `:has(:is(#a, .b))`. This function takes a relative selector and scores as the most specific argument, comparing identifier count first, then class count, then type count, and the part of the selector outside the function is added on top. Give the triple for each of the five, in that order.

options.text: Zero, one, zero then one, zero, zero then zero, one, one then zero, one, two then one, zero, zero
Zero, zero, zero then zero, zero, zero then zero, one, one then zero, one, two then zero, zero, zero
options.misconception: believes a relative pseudo-class adds nothing of its own and its argument is not counted

options.text: Zero, one, zero then one, zero, zero then zero, zero, one then zero, one, one then one, zero, zero
options.misconception: believes a leading child combinator inside the argument adds a type column

options.text: One, one, zero then one, zero, zero then zero, one, one then one, one, two then one, zero, zero
options.misconception: believes the class outside the function in the fourth selector is counted twice

questions.explanation: The relative-argument function scores as the most specific thing its argument can match, and the leading combinator inside the argument contributes nothing of its own because it names a relationship rather than a part. So the first selector takes one class column, the second takes one identifier column, and the fifth takes the identifier inside the nested matching function, giving one, zero, zero. The third adds the type selector outside the function to the class column from inside it, giving zero, one, one, and the fourth is the interesting one because the argument contains two type selectors and a class, so it contributes one class and two type columns, which the surrounding list item then adds a third type column to, giving zero, one, two. The third option is the mistake people make with the child combinator: it changes what the argument can match and not what it is worth. The practical consequence is the same as for the other functional pseudo-classes, namely that a rule written this way is far more specific than its readability suggests, so it needs a deliberate reason for the argument it names.
questions.hint: Score the argument as if the combinator inside it were not there, then add the part of the selector that is outside the function.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: The score an attribute selector and its case flag contribute
questions.learningObjective: compute the specificity of attribute selectors and read the effect of the case flag
questions.stem: A resolver is asked for the specificity of eight selectors: `[data-x]`, `[data-x="y"]`, `[data-x="y" i]`, `[class~="a"]`, `[href^="https"]`, `[href$=".pdf"]`, `[src*="logo"]` and `a[href][target]`. It then matches four selectors against an anchor whose attribute value is an upper-case word and prints the matches. Give the two answers: the specificity of the eight selectors, and which of the three case-flagged comparisons against that anchor succeed.

options.text: All eight are zero, zero, zero because an attribute selector matches on data rather than on a name, and the case-insensitive comparisons both succeed
options.misconception: believes an attribute selector contributes nothing to the score

options.text: The first seven are zero, one, zero and the last is zero, one, one because the two attribute selectors share a class column, and the case-insensitive comparisons both succeed
options.misconception: believes two attribute selectors in one compound share one class column

options.text: All eight are zero, one, zero except the last which is zero, two, one, and the case-insensitive exact match fails because the value differs in case
options.misconception: believes the case flag does not affect an exact comparison

options.text: All eight are zero, one, zero except the last which is zero, two, one, and the case-insensitive exact match succeeds while the case-insensitive prefix match against a different word does not

questions.explanation: An attribute selector is scored as a class selector, so each one adds exactly one to the middle column regardless of which operator it uses and regardless of any flag. That is why the first seven all come out as zero, one, zero, and it is also why the last one, which is a type selector followed by two attribute selectors, comes out as one type column and two class columns: the two attributes add two, not one, because each is counted separately. The case flag changes matching and not scoring, which is the point of the second half of the question. With an upper-case value present, the case-sensitive exact comparison against a lower-case text fails because the values are different strings, and the case-insensitive version of the same comparison succeeds because the flag folds case on both sides. A case-insensitive prefix comparison against a different word still fails, because folding case does not make one word a prefix of another. The two halves together are the useful lesson: the flag is free in score terms and expensive in surprise terms, because it turns a selector that matches almost nothing into one that matches a case variant it was never written for.
questions.hint: Every attribute selector adds one to the class column, and the case flag changes which values match without changing the count.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: The score a positional pseudo-class contributes
questions.learningObjective: compute the specificity of positional and counting pseudo-classes
questions.stem: A resolver is asked for the specificity of seven selectors: `li:nth-child(2)`, `li:nth-child(2n+1)`, `li:nth-of-type(2)`, `li:nth-child(2n+1 of .x)`, `li:nth-last-child(1)`, `li:first-child` and `li:nth-child(odd)`. A plain positional pseudo-class adds one to the class column, and a counting one adds one to the class column plus whatever the list it filters by is worth. Give the triple for each of the seven, in that order.

options.text: Zero, one, one for all seven, because the filter list inside a counting pseudo-class does not reach the score
options.misconception: believes the filter list is ignored by the specificity calculation

options.text: Zero, one, one for the first three, then zero, one, two, then zero, one, one for the last three
options.misconception: believes the filter list contributes to the type column

options.text: Zero, one, one for the first three, then zero, two, one, then zero, one, one for the last three
Zero, zero, one for the first three, then zero, one, one, then zero, zero, one for the last three
options.misconception: believes a positional pseudo-class contributes to the type column

questions.explanation: Every plain positional pseudo-class in the list behaves the same way: it adds one to the class column and the surrounding list item adds one to the type column, giving zero, one, one. That covers the first three and the last three, and the presence of a formula like two n plus one or the word odd changes nothing about the score, only about which positions match. The fourth is the one that differs, because it carries a filter list naming a class, and that class is scored like any other class selector and added on top of the pseudo-class's own contribution, so the class column becomes two. The second option is the mistake the specification went out of its way to close: the filter list is part of what the selector can match, so leaving it out of the score would let a list of arbitrary complexity cost nothing. The practical note is that positional selectors are cheap in score but expensive in coupling, because they describe a position in a parent that the markup is free to reorder, so a rule written this way changes behaviour when an unrelated item is inserted above it.
questions.hint: Count the pseudo-class as one class, add the filter list if there is one, and add the surrounding type selector.

questions.topic: What the universal selector and the combinators contribute
questions.learningObjective: compute the specificity of selectors built from combinators and the universal selector
questions.stem: A resolver is asked for the specificity of ten selectors: `*`, `* div`, `div *`, `div > *`, `div p`, `div > p`, `div + p`, `div ~ p`, `*.card` and `div.card`. Neither a combinator nor the universal selector contributes anything. Give the triple for each of the ten, in that order.

options.text: Zero, zero, zero then one, one, one three times, then one, one, two three times, then one, one, zero then one, one, one
options.misconception: believes a combinator adds one to each of the two columns it joins

options.text: Zero, zero, zero then zero, zero, one three times, then zero, zero, two three times, then zero, one, zero then zero, one, one
Zero, zero, zero then zero, zero, one three times, then zero, zero, two three times, then zero, one, zero then zero, zero, one
options.misconception: believes a class selector after a type selector adds to the type column

options.text: Zero, zero, zero then zero, zero, zero then zero, zero, one then zero, zero, two then zero, one, zero then zero, one, one
options.misconception: believes a type selector after a combinator is not counted

questions.explanation: The universal selector on its own scores nothing at all, and that is the first result. A combinator is a relationship rather than a part, so the four selectors that differ only in their combinator all score the same: a type selector on each side of the relationship gives zero, zero, two, and the child, adjacent and general-sibling forms are indistinguishable in score even though they match different elements. Adding a class changes the column it belongs to, so the universal selector followed by a class gives zero, one, zero while a type selector followed by a class gives zero, one, one, and the difference of one in the last column is the type selector that the first of the pair does not have. The practical point is that a combinator is free, which is what makes a descendant selector cheap to write, and that the difference between the child form and the descendant form is a matching question rather than a scoring one, so the same score can be spent on very different amounts of the document.
questions.hint: Score only the parts of the selector; a relationship between them is not a part.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Choosing the winning declaration among three rules on one element
questions.learningObjective: trace which of three matching declarations the cascade selects and why
questions.stem: A stylesheet holds, in this order, `p { color: black }`, `.note { color: teal }` and `p.note { color: gray }`. The document has one paragraph carrying the note class. A resolver is run against it and prints the winning colour together with the selector that produced it. What does it print?

options.text: Gray from the two-part selector, because it scores zero, one, one and beats the one-part class selector on the type column
Teal from the class selector, because a class selector is more specific than any selector that also names a type
options.misconception: believes a type selector in a compound adds nothing to the score

options.text: Black from the type selector, because the earliest rule wins whenever a class selector is present
options.misconception: believes source order alone decides between rules of different scores

options.text: Gray from the two-part selector, because it appears last in the sheet
options.misconception: believes the last matching declaration always wins regardless of score

questions.explanation: All three rules match the element, so the decision comes down to the three columns read left to right. The type-only rule scores zero, zero, one and the class-only rule scores zero, one, zero, so the class rule wins that pair on the second column before the third is consulted. The two-part rule scores zero, one, one, which ties the class rule on the first two columns and beats it on the third, so the two-part rule wins. Source order is never reached, because two declarations are only separated by their order when their scores are equal in every column, which is the point the fourth option misses: the last declaration in the sheet does not win, it wins only when the earlier one was equally entitled. The three columns exist so that this is decidable without reading the whole sheet, and the usual mistake is a two-part selector that a developer assumed was weaker because it has fewer characters, when its score is actually the highest of the three.
questions.hint: Score all three, then compare the columns from the left and use the sheet order only if every column ties.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Reading the declaration order a set of layers produces
questions.learningObjective: trace the winner among three rules once each is placed in a named layer
questions.stem: A sheet opens with `@layer base, components, utilities;` and then defines, in that order, a base layer rule setting the colour black, a components layer rule setting it blue, and a utilities layer rule setting it green, all on a paragraph. A resolver is run with the layer order taken from the opening statement and prints the winning colour and the layer it came from. What does it print?

options.text: Black from the base layer, because the first layer declared is the strongest
options.misconception: believes the first layer declared outranks the later ones

options.text: Blue from the components layer, because the middle layer is the one intended to win over the base
options.misconception: believes a middle layer is special

options.text: Green from the utilities layer, because it appears last in the sheet rather than because of the layer order
options.misconception: believes the winning layer rule won on position in the source

options.text: Green from the utilities layer, because a later layer outranks an earlier one regardless of how specific the earlier rule is

questions.explanation: A layer is consulted before the score, so the three rules never reach the column comparison at all. The opening statement fixes the order, and in that order the base layer is weakest and the utilities layer is strongest, so the utilities rule wins whatever its selector is. The opening statement matters because without it the order would be the order of first appearance in the sheet, and any layer named in a statement has to be registered before it is used, so declaring the order up front is how a stylesheet guarantees it rather than leaving it to the order rules happen to be written in. The distinction between the first and fourth options is worth being precise about: they give the same colour here, and the difference is the reason. If the base rule had been the more specific selector, the answer would still be green, because the layer comparison comes first; the fourth option's explanation would then be wrong even though its answer was right, which is the sort of explanation that misleads the next person to debug it.
questions.hint: Compare the layer ranks first; only rules in the same layer go on to the score comparison.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: The layer order an important declaration ends up using
questions.learningObjective: trace how importance reverses the ranking of layered declarations
questions.stem: A sheet opens with `@layer a, b;` and then holds a rule in layer a setting the colour red with importance, a rule in layer b setting it blue with importance, and an unlayered rule setting it green without importance. The element is a plain paragraph, so all three match. A resolver prints the winning colour. What does it print, and what is the general rule that produces it?

options.text: Green, because an unlayered rule outranks every layered rule however the layers are marked
options.misconception: believes the unlayered advantage applies to important declarations too

options.text: Blue, because the last layer declared wins among important declarations as it does among normal ones
options.misconception: believes importance changes which declarations win but not the layer order

options.text: Red, because importance moves the whole group above every normal declaration and then reverses the layer order so the earliest layer wins
Red, because the important rule with the highest score wins, and the score beats the layer order
options.misconception: believes score comparison happens before layer comparison for important declarations

questions.explanation: Importance is checked before everything else in the same origin, so the two marked declarations leave the contest against the unlayered normal one before any comparison of layers or scores happens. Within the important group the layer order is reversed, and the reversal is the deliberate design of the feature: if the normal order made the last layer the strongest, an important declaration in the first layer would be powerless, which is the opposite of what importance is for. So the earliest layer wins among important declarations, which is red here. The two distractors are both real rules applied in the wrong place. The unlayered advantage over layers is a rule about normal declarations and does not survive importance. The score comparison is consulted only among declarations in the same layer, so the fourth option's mechanism cannot be the reason, and it would give the wrong answer the moment the two important rules were in the same layer with different scores.
questions.hint: Check importance first, then remember that importance reverses which end of the layer order is stronger.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: What an important declaration outranks in its own origin
questions.learningObjective: compare an important declaration against a more specific normal one in two cases
questions.stem: A sheet holds `#x { color: red }` and then `p { color: blue }` with importance, and the element is a paragraph carrying the identifier. A resolver prints the winning colour. The sheet is then changed so both declarations carry importance, and the resolver is run again on the same element. What does each run print?

options.text: Red on both runs, because a selector with an identifier outranks any declaration on the same element
options.misconception: believes an identifier outranks importance in the same origin

options.text: Blue on the first run and red on the second, because importance is checked before score and the reversal leaves the score comparison in charge
Blue on the first run and blue on the second, because the later declaration wins whenever importance appears anywhere in the sheet
options.misconception: believes importance in one rule promotes every later rule

options.text: Blue on the first run and red on the second, because importance is checked before score and the first rule's position in the sheet then decides
options.misconception: believes the score comparison is replaced by source order for important declarations

questions.explanation: On the first run the important declaration wins even though its selector is much weaker, because the order of checks puts importance ahead of score: the two declarations are not compared on score at all, only on importance, and the one that carries it is the only one left. On the second run both carry importance, so the importance check separates nothing and the comparison falls through to the score, where the identifier wins because the first column decides before the sheet order is consulted. The fourth option gets the first run right and then describes the second one wrongly, which is the more damaging kind of wrong: the score comparison is not replaced by source order when importance is present, it simply becomes the deciding comparison. That is also why importance is a poor tool in a stylesheet nobody owns alone, since a single marked rule silently outranks every other rule for that property until it is removed.
questions.hint: Ask whether the importance check separates the two declarations before you compare anything else.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Why an unlayered rule outranks every layered rule
questions.learningObjective: trace the winner when a layered and an unlayered declaration both match
questions.practice: tracing the unlayered tier of the cascade
questions.stem: A sheet holds a rule inside the last of three named layers setting the colour blue, and then an unlayered rule setting it green. The element is a plain paragraph. A resolver prints the winning colour. What does it print, and what is the design reason for the outcome?

options.text: Green, because an unlayered rule is ranked above every layer, which is what lets a sheet override its own layers deliberately
Blue, because the last named layer is the strongest tier in the cascade
options.misconception: believes the last layer outranks rules outside any layer

options.text: Green, because the unlayered rule appears later in the sheet than the layered one
options.misconception: believes the unlayered rule won on its position in the source

options.text: Blue, because a rule inside a layer block is treated as if it were nested and is therefore more specific
options.misconception: believes being inside a block adds to the score

questions.explanation: The unlayered tier sits above every named layer, so a declaration outside any layer beats a declaration inside one however specific the layered one is and whichever layer it is in. The design reason is the one the fourth option gets wrong: a layer block is a naming construct and adds nothing to the score, so the layered rule's advantage over the other layered rules is entirely the layer order. The unlayered tier exists so that a stylesheet that needs to beat its own layered system can do so without renaming anything or resorting to importance, which is the escape hatch that keeps a layered architecture from becoming a trap. The third option gets the colour right and the reason wrong, and that distinction is the whole value of the question, because a developer who believes the unlayered rule won on position will not understand why moving it to the top of the sheet changes nothing.
questions.hint: Ask where an unlayered declaration is ranked relative to the last named layer, and separately ask whether a layer block changes the score.

questions.stem: A resolver is asked for the specificity of `p::before { content: "" }`, `a:hover::after { content: "" }`, `li::marker { content: "" }` and `p::first-letter { font-weight: bold }`. A pseudo-element adds one to the type column, and the selector before it is counted normally. Give the triple for each of the four, in that order.

options.text: Zero, one, one then one, one, one then zero, one, one then zero, one, one
options.misconception: believes a pseudo-element adds to the class column

options.text: Zero, one, one then one, one, one then zero, one, one then zero, one, one
options.misconception: believes a pseudo-element does not count at all

options.text: Zero, zero, one then zero, one, one then zero, zero, one then zero, one, one
options.misconception: believes a state pseudo-class before a pseudo-element adds an identifier column

options.text: Zero, zero, two then zero, one, two then zero, zero, two then zero, zero, two

questions.explanation: A pseudo-element occupies the type column, which is why every one of these four has at least one there and none has more than one. The plain type selector plus the pseudo-element gives two type columns, and a state pseudo-class in between contributes a class column, so the second selector is the one with a class column in it. The third is a bare type selector plus the pseudo-element, so it has no class column at all, and the fourth is the same shape as the first, so it also has two type columns and no class column. The distinction the question turns on is that a state pseudo-class scores as a class while a pseudo-element scores as a type, and they can appear next to each other in the same compound. That matters in practice because generated content is the one part of a box a rule cannot otherwise reach, so the only way to style it is through a rule that ends in a pseudo-element, and the two columns that rule draws on are the same two any other selector uses.
questions.hint: Count the pseudo-element as a type selector, and count a state pseudo-class before it as a class selector.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Which properties a descendant picks up and which it has to be given
questions.learningObjective: classify a list of properties by whether a descendant takes them from its parent
questions.stem: A parent element has a stylesheet setting its colour, font size, line height, visibility, top border width, top margin, left padding, display, position, stacking order, opacity, font family, text alignment, overflow, width and transform. A child element has no stylesheet of its own. The program prints, for each property, whether the child takes the parent's value or not. Which properties are on the inherited side of that list?

options.text: Colour, font size, line height, visibility, font family, text alignment, display and position, and the remaining eight are set from their initial values
options.misconception: believes a layout property is inherited because the child needs a display value

options.text: Every property on the list is inherited, because a child element takes its parent's whole computed style
options.misconception: believes inheritance transfers the entire computed style

options.text: Colour, font size, line height, visibility, font family and text alignment, and the remaining ten are set on the child from their initial values
Colour, font size, line height, visibility, font family and text alignment but not the top border width, and the box and layout properties are inherited as well
options.misconception: believes a border is inherited but a box size is not

questions.explanation: Inheritance is per property, and the dividing line is whether the property describes the text inside the box or the box itself. Colour, font size, line height, visibility, font family and text alignment all describe rendered text, so a child that has no rule of its own uses the parent's value, and that is what makes a heading inside a body look like body text at a different weight rather than reverting to the browser default. Everything else on the list describes the box or its placement, and those start from their own initial values on the child: a border, a margin, a padding, a display, a position, a stacking order, an opacity, an overflow, a width and a transform. The second option is the intuition behind the mistake, that a child must have a display value and so must be inheriting one, but the child's display is its own, and inheriting a parent's block value into a child that should be a paragraph is exactly the kind of bug inheritance is designed to avoid. The fourth option has the border backwards: a border belongs to the box that draws it, which is why no child ever grows a border just because its parent has one.
questions.hint: Ask whether the property describes the text inside the box or the box itself; only the first kind is inherited.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: The outer width a declared width produces under each sizing rule
questions.learningObjective: compute the outer width of a box under both sizing rules and the width that reaches a target
questions.practice: computing outer width under both sizing rules
questions.stem: A box declares a width of 300, padding of 20 on each side and a border of 2 on each side. The program computes the outer width under the initial sizing rule, then under the alternative one, and then computes the width a box must declare to reach an outer width of 300 under each rule. What are the three numbers for each rule?

options.text: Under the initial rule the declared width is 256 and the outer width is 300, and 344 declared reaches 300; under the alternative rule the declared width is 300 and the outer width is 344, and 256 declared reaches 300
options.misconception: believes the two rules differ only in which number the author writes

options.text: Under the initial rule the declared width is 300 and the outer width is 344, and 300 declared reaches an outer width of 344; under the alternative rule the declared width is 300 and the outer width is 300, and 300 declared reaches 300
Under both rules the declared width is 300 and the outer width is 344, because padding and border are added outside the box either way
options.misconception: believes the alternative rule still adds padding and border outside the declared width

options.text: Under the initial rule the declared width is 300 and the outer width is 300, and under the alternative rule the declared width is 344 and the outer width is 300
options.misconception: believes the initial rule already includes padding and border

questions.explanation: The initial sizing rule declares the content width, so a declared 300 is the distance from the inner edge of one border to the inner edge of the other, and the padding and the border are added outside it: twenty on each side of the content is forty, plus two on each side of the padding is four, so the box occupies 344 and the content is still 300. The alternative rule declares the width of the box itself, so a declared 300 is the outer width and the content has the forty and the four taken out of it, leaving 256. That is what makes a percentage width usable: a box declared as a percentage of its parent would overflow under the initial rule as soon as it had any padding, and the arithmetic in the second option shows the two rules are not merely relabelled but genuinely different, since the same declared number means a different box under each. The third and fourth options each get one of the two rules right and the other wrong, which is the shape of the confusion this item is for.
questions.hint: Ask which edge of the box the declared width measures to, then add or subtract padding and the border accordingly.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: The length a percentage padding resolves to
questions.learningObjective: compute a percentage padding against several containing block widths
questions.stem: Four boxes sit inside containing blocks of 800, 800, 400 and 360 units, and each declares a padding of 10, 5, 10 and 2.5 percent respectively. The program prints, for each, the padding on one side and the total padding across the inline direction. What does it print?

options.text: Eighty and one hundred and sixty, then forty and eighty, then forty and eighty, then nine and eighteen
Eighty and eighty, then forty and forty, then forty and forty, then nine and nine
options.misconception: believes a percentage padding is already the total across both sides

options.text: Eight and sixteen, then four and eight, then four and eight, then zero point nine and one point eight
options.misconception: believes the percentage is taken against the padding of the element

options.text: Eighty and one hundred and sixty, then forty and eighty, then forty and eighty, then nine and nine
options.misconception: believes the total is the same for every case regardless of the fractional part

questions.explanation: A percentage padding is taken against the inline size of the containing block, not against the element's own width and not against the padding, which rules out the third option immediately. So the first box's ten percent of 800 is 80 on each side and 160 across the inline direction, the second box's five percent of 800 is 40 and 80, the third box's ten percent of 400 is 40 and 80, and the fourth box's two and a half percent of 360 is 9 and 18. The fourth case is the one that catches people out: the fraction is applied to the whole number and then not rounded at this stage, so two and a half percent of 360 is exactly nine and the total is eighteen, not the eighteen-point-something the mental arithmetic suggests and not the same total as the third case. The last point is that a percentage padding does not scale with the element, so a row of cards whose width is set by the grid still has padding that follows the row, which is why a fluid layout with percentage padding grows its gutters as the viewport widens.
questions.hint: Take the percentage of the containing block's inline size and double it for the inline total.

questions.topic: The height a ratio computes from a width, and the case where it does not
questions.learningObjective: compute a box height from a declared ratio and identify the case where the ratio is ignored
questions.practice: computing a height from a ratio
questions.stem: Four stylesheet rules are evaluated: `.a { width: 320; aspect-ratio: 16 / 9 }`, `.b { width: 300; aspect-ratio: 1 / 1 }`, `.c { width: 640; aspect-ratio: 4 / 3 }` and `.d { width: 300; height: 200; aspect-ratio: 3 / 2 }`. A ratio supplies a dimension that was not given and leaves a dimension that was. The program prints the height each rule ends up with. What does it print?

options.text: One hundred and eighty, then three hundred, then four hundred and eighty, then one hundred and fifty because the ratio overrides the declared height
options.misconception: believes a ratio replaces a declared height even when one is given

options.text: One hundred and eighty, then one hundred and two hundred, then three hundred and twenty, then two hundred
options.misconception: believes a ratio is inverted, so the height is the width times the ratio

options.text: One hundred and eighty, then three hundred, then six hundred and forty, then two hundred
options.misconception: believes a ratio of four to three gives a height equal to the width

options.text: One hundred and eighty, then three hundred, then four hundred and eighty, then two hundred unchanged because both dimensions are already definite

questions.explanation: A ratio supplies the missing dimension, so a box with a width and no height takes the height that makes the two agree: 320 divided by sixteen to nine is 180, 300 divided by one is 300, and 640 divided by four to three is 480. The fourth box is the case the item turns on. A ratio only fills in a dimension that was not given, and here both were given, so the declared height of 200 stands and the ratio has nothing left to do. That is why a box that already has a height from its content, as a box holding text usually does, will not be forced into the ratio: the ratio is a hint for a missing dimension, not a constraint on a present one. The third option inverts the arithmetic, and it is worth checking which way the ratio is written, because a ratio of sixteen to nine is sixteen units wide for every nine units tall, and reading it the other way round is the most common single error in this area.
questions.hint: Divide the width by the ratio, and check whether a height was already declared before the ratio gets a say.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: The value a three-argument minimum function picks at one width
questions.learningObjective: evaluate the minimum, maximum and clamping functions at a stated viewport width
questions.practice: evaluating clamp at a stated width
questions.stem: The viewport is 500 wide and 800 tall, the root font size is 16 and the element font size is 16, and the reference box the percentage resolves against is 400 in both viewports. Four rules are evaluated: `.a { width: min(50%, 300px) }`, `.b { max-width: max(20em, 300px) }`, `.c { width: clamp(1rem, 5vw, 40rem) }` and `.d { width: clamp(200px, 5vw, 400px) }`. The program prints the four resolved widths, then the same four expressions at a viewport 1200 wide. What does it print?

options.text: Three hundred, 320, 25 and 400 in the first viewport, and 300, 320, 60 and 400 in the second
options.misconception: believes the clamping function returns whichever bound is nearest

options.text: Two hundred, 300, 400 and 200 in the first viewport, and 200, 300, 400 and 200 in the second
options.misconception: believes an em is measured against the root font size rather than the element's own

options.text: Two hundred, 320, 25 and 200 in the first viewport, and 200, 320, 60 and 200 in the second
Two hundred and fifty, 320, 25 and 200 in the first viewport, and 250, 320, 60 and 200 in the second
options.misconception: believes fifty percent of 500 is taken rather than fifty percent of the reference

questions.explanation: Each expression is resolved before the outer function picks, and only two of the four expressions respond to the viewport at all. Fifty percent of the 400 reference is 200, so the minimum of 200 and 300 is 200 in both viewports, because a percentage argument resolves against the reference box rather than against the viewport. Twenty em at an element font size of 16 is 320, so the maximum of 320 and 300 is 320 in both, because the element font size did not change. One rem is 16 and forty rems is 640, and five percent of the viewport is 25 at 500 wide and 60 at 1200 wide; in both cases that value already sits between the two bounds, so the middle value is taken and this is the first expression that actually moves. The fourth expression is the same shape with the middle value still below its lower bound of 200 at both widths, so the lower bound is taken and it never moves either. The second option is the misconception the clamping function is most often confused with: it is not a choice between the bounds but a clamp around the preferred value, which is why its middle argument is written as a fluid length in the first place.
questions.hint: Convert every argument to one unit first, then apply the outer function to the numbers.

questions.topic: The line box a font size and a line height produce
questions.learningObjective: compute the line box height, the half leading and the first baseline from a font size and a line height
questions.stem: A block of text has a font size of 16 and wraps onto three lines. In the first case the line height is given as the number one and a half and in the second as 24 units. The program prints, for each case, the resolved line box height, the half leading, the distance from the top of the first line box to the first baseline, and the total height of the three lines. What does it print?

options.text: Twenty-four, four, twenty and seventy-two in the first case, and twenty-four, minus eight, eight and seventy-two in the second
options.misconception: believes a length is measured relative to the font size the way a number is

options.text: Twenty-four, four, twenty and seventy-two in both cases, because a bare number and a matching length resolve to the same line box
Sixteen, zero, sixteen and forty-eight in the first case, and twenty-four, four, twenty and seventy-two in the second
options.misconception: believes a bare line height number is used as a length in the element's own units

options.text: Twenty-four, four, twenty and seventy-two in the first case, and sixteen, zero, sixteen and forty-eight in the second
options.misconception: believes a line height given as a length is capped at the font size

questions.explanation: A bare number is a multiplier of the element's own font size, so 1.5 at a font size of 16 resolves to 24, and a line height written as 24 units is used exactly as written, so the two cases coincide. From there the arithmetic is the same in both: the line box is 24 tall, the difference between the line box and the content area of the text is 24 minus 16, and half of that is 4, so 4 units of space sits above the content and 4 below it. The first baseline is therefore 4 plus the font size, which is 20 from the top of the line box, and three lines are 72 tall. The distinction the item is really about is the difference between a number and a length, and it matters the moment a child changes the font size: a bare number travels with the font and the spacing scales, while a length does not, so a line height written as a number keeps a fixed proportion across a heading and its body text and one written as a length keeps the same absolute leading everywhere.
questions.hint: Resolve the line height to a length, then the rest follows from the difference between it and the font size.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: What a cascade layer adds to the order of decisions
questions.learningObjective: explain what a cascade layer contributes to the sequence of checks the engine makes
questions.practice: explaining the purpose of a cascade layer
questions.stem: A design system ships a base layer, a components layer and a utilities layer, and an application stylesheet is told to put anything it needs to beat the components layer into a layer of its own. What does a layer contribute to the sequence of checks, and what problem does it solve that a higher score cannot?

options.text: A layer is compared before the score is, so a rule in a later layer wins whatever its selector, and the problem it solves is that score cannot be raised without writing a more specific selector
A layer is compared after the score is, so it only breaks ties between rules of equal score, and the problem it solves is that ties were being decided by sheet order
options.misconception: believes a layer only matters when two selectors score the same

options.text: A layer replaces the score entirely, so every rule in the same layer is decided by sheet order alone
options.misconception: believes being in the same layer removes the score comparison

options.text: A layer is compared before the score is and replaces the score as well, so a rule in a later layer wins and a rule in an earlier one never applies
options.misconception: believes a layer removes the score comparison entirely

questions.explanation: The order of checks is importance, then layer, then score, then sheet order, and a layer sits above the score precisely so that a sheet can beat a component without writing a selector uglier than the component's own. That is the problem it solves. Without it, the only ways to win are a more specific selector, which is a permanent tax on everyone who has to override you later, or importance, which outranks every rule in the origin including the ones written afterwards. A layer is a declaration of intent: it says this is an override layer, and it costs one line at the top of the sheet. The second option understates it, because if a layer only broke ties it would be a way of writing the sheet order more verbosely. The third and fourth options both misdescribe what happens inside a layer, where the score and then the sheet order still decide, and the fourth adds a claim that an earlier layer stops applying, which would make the base layer of every design system dead code.
questions.hint: Write the four checks in the order the engine makes them and see where the layer comparison lands.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Why a more specific rule cannot escape from an earlier layer
questions.learningObjective: explain why raising a selector's score does not help it win against a later layer
questions.practice: explaining the limit of specificity inside a layered sheet
questions.stem: A stylesheet puts an identifier selector in its first named layer and a class selector in its last, and both set the same property on the same element. The class selector loses even when the identifier selector is given two identifiers and three classes. Why, and what would the developer have to reach for instead?

options.text: The score comparison comes first, so the identifier selector should have won and the sheet is misconfigured
options.misconception: believes the sheet order is score first and layer second

options.text: A selector may carry at most one identifier, so the extra ones were discarded and the two rules ended up tied on score
options.misconception: believes a selector is limited to a single identifier

options.text: Layers are resolved per property and this property was never registered in the later layer, so the later declaration was dropped
options.misconception: believes a layer applies to some properties and not others

options.text: The layer comparison comes first, so the earlier layer is outranked no matter how high its score goes, and the developer has to move the declaration into a later layer or out of any layer

questions.explanation: The comparison of layer ranks happens before any comparison of scores, so a declaration in an earlier layer is eliminated whatever its selector is, and the two extra identifiers and three classes in this case were never counted because they were never needed. That is the whole design of the feature: it makes the score irrelevant across a layer boundary so that the layer order, which is written down once and is readable, is what governs the override story. The developer's two routes are both legitimate and both cost something. Moving the declaration into a later layer is the clean one and is what the layer order was declared for. Writing it outside every layer is the blunt one, since the unlayered tier sits above all of them, and it is the escape hatch that lets a single rule override a whole system at the cost of no longer being reorderable by anyone else. Importance is the third route and the worst of the three here, because it outranks every later normal rule for that property as well.
questions.hint: Ask at which point in the sequence the layer ranks are compared relative to the score, and what follows from that ordering.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: What importance changes about the layer order and what it leaves alone
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the effect of importance on the layer order from its effect on the score
questions.stem: Two rules sit in two named layers, the earlier one carrying importance and the later one not, and both set the same property. Separately, two important rules sit in the same layer with different scores. What does importance do in each case, and what does it leave untouched?

options.text: It promotes the important declaration above every normal one in the origin and also raises its score above every other score, so the two important rules in one layer are decided by importance alone
options.misconception: believes importance adds a component to the score

options.text: It reverses the layer order for the important declaration and leaves the score comparison untouched, so an important rule in an earlier layer beats a normal rule in a later one only on score
options.misconception: believes a normal rule in a later layer can still outrank an important one in an earlier layer

options.text: It promotes the important declaration above every normal one in the origin, reverses which end of the layer order is stronger among important ones, and leaves the score comparison in charge between important rules in the same layer
It leaves the layer order alone and only raises the declaration above normal ones, so among important declarations the last layer still wins
options.misconception: believes importance has no effect on the layer order

questions.explanation: Importance is checked first, so it removes every normal declaration in the same origin from the contest before the layer ranks or the scores are compared at all. Within the important group the layer order is read in reverse, which is deliberate: if the last layer were still the strongest, an important declaration written in a component layer could never beat a normal one in a utilities layer, and importance would be nearly useless for the overrides it exists to enable. The score comparison is untouched, so two important rules in the same layer are decided exactly as two normal rules would be, by their scores and then by their sheet order. The second option is the commonest misreading, arising from a picture of importance as a fourth column; it is not a column and adding one would make an important rule beat every later important rule, which is not what the mechanism does. The fourth option is the opposite error, and the third contradicts the first check.
questions.hint: List the four checks in order, then ask which of them importance changes and which it leaves as it was.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Which declarations open a new stacking context
questions.learningObjective: sort a list of computed declarations into those that open a stacking context and those that do not
questions.stem: Six elements are given one declaration each. The first is positioned with an explicit stacking order, the second is positioned with no stacking order, the third is unpositioned with a stacking order, the fourth is unpositioned with a full opacity, the fifth is unpositioned with a transform, and the sixth is unpositioned with an isolated blend grouping. Which of the six open a new stacking context?

options.text: All six, because a stacking order opens a stacking context whatever the element's position
options.misconception: believes a stacking order alone is enough on an unpositioned element

options.text: The first, the fourth, the fifth and the sixth, and not the second or the third, so a stacking order on an unpositioned element does nothing on its own
The first, the second, the fourth and the sixth, and not the third or the fifth, so a transform is not one of the triggers
options.misconception: believes a transform leaves the painting order of siblings unchanged

options.text: The first and the third, and not the others, because only a stacking order can open a stacking context
options.misconception: believes opacity, transform and blend grouping have no effect on painting order

questions.explanation: A stacking context is opened either by a position that is not the default combined with an explicit stacking order, or by one of a list of properties that change how the element composites. The first element is in the first group, so it opens one. The second is positioned but has no explicit order, and a positioned element with no order participates in its parent's context rather than opening its own, which is why it is excluded. The third has an order but is unpositioned, and the same rule applies in reverse: the order is stored as a computed value and has no effect on its own, so the element paints as an ordinary in-flow box. The fourth, fifth and sixth are all unpositioned and all open a context anyway, because a reduced opacity, a transform and an isolated blend grouping each force the element to be composited separately, and that is exactly what the rule is telling the engine to do. A transform has the further consequence of becoming the containing block for fixed descendants, which is the trap that catches people out.
questions.hint: Split the six into the position-and-order pair and the property list, and check each element against both groups.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: The order children are painted in inside one stacking context
questions.learningObjective: sort sibling boxes into the painting order of a single stacking context
questions.stem: One element opens a stacking context and has eight children: a positioned child with a stacking order of three, an ordinary block child, a positioned child with a stacking order of minus one, a floated child, an inline child, a positioned child with no stacking order, a child with a reduced opacity, and a positioned child with a stacking order of one. What is the painting order from the bottom up?

options.text: The minus one child, the block, the float, the inline, the no-order positioned child, the reduced-opacity child, then the one and then the three
The block, the float, the inline, the minus one child, the no-order positioned child, the reduced-opacity child, then the three and then the one
options.misconception: believes a negative stacking order still paints above the in-flow content

options.text: The minus one child, the block, the float, the inline, the no-order positioned child, then the three, then the one, then the reduced-opacity child
options.misconception: believes a child that opens its own context is painted last regardless of its order

options.text: The block, the float, the inline, the minus one child, the no-order positioned child, the three, the one, then the reduced-opacity child
options.misconception: believes a positive stacking order sorts in the reverse of the numeric value

questions.explanation: Painting inside a stacking context runs in a fixed sequence of steps, and the eight children in this item land in six of them. The backgrounds and borders of the context's own element go first, then any child that opens a context with a negative order, which is the minus one child, then the in-flow non-positioned block descendants, then the floats, then the inline content, then the positioned descendants and the children that opened a context with a zero or absent order, in tree order, and finally the children with positive orders from smallest to largest. The two positive children therefore go in with one before three, and the reduced-opacity child is in the middle group because a reduced opacity opens a context with no order, so it sorts by tree order rather than by any number. The fourth option has the positive sort reversed, which is the one thing about this sequence that is counter-intuitive enough to be worth stating explicitly: larger positive values are painted later and so appear on top.
questions.hint: Work down the fixed sequence of painting steps and place each child in the first step that claims it.

questions.topic: Why a large stacking order on a child cannot lift it out of its parent's group
questions.learningObjective: explain why a descendant's stacking order is confined to the context its ancestor opened
questions.practice: explaining the limit of a descendant stacking order
questions.stem: A card is given a reduced opacity, which makes it open a stacking context, and a child inside the card is given a stacking order of nine hundred and ninety-nine. A sibling of the card is positioned with a stacking order of one. Which paints on top, and what would the card have to give up for the child to win?

options.text: The child paints on top, because a stacking order is compared with every sibling in the document rather than only with the context's own children
options.misconception: believes a stacking order reaches beyond the nearest context

options.text: The sibling paints on top, because a stacking order is only honoured for positioned elements and the child is unpositioned
options.misconception: believes the child lost because of its position rather than because of its ancestor

options.text: Both paint at the same level, because a context formed by a reduced opacity sorts its children in tree order regardless of their orders
options.misconception: believes a reduced-opacity context ignores the orders of its children

options.text: The sibling paints on top, because the card's context sorts the child as part of the card, and the card would have to stop opening a context for the child to be compared with the sibling

questions.explanation: A stacking order is only ever compared with the other members of the same stacking context, and a reduced opacity makes the card one, so the child's order of nine hundred and ninety-nine is compared with the card's other children and then the card is placed as a unit. The card itself has no order, so it sorts with the group of positioned descendants and context-forming children of its own parent, and the sibling with an order of one is in that group too, where tree order decides. The child therefore cannot rise above the sibling no matter how large its number is, which is the correct behaviour: an order that escaped its context would make the context pointless. The price of winning is the card's own effect, because the only way for the child to be compared with the sibling is for the card to stop opening a context, which for this card means dropping the reduced opacity. The second option describes a mental model in which orders are global, and the fourth is wrong because the context does sort its children by order, just not beyond itself.
questions.hint: Ask which elements are members of the same stacking context as the child, and which are members of the context as the card.

questions.topic: What a transform does to the box a fixed descendant is placed against
questions.learningObjective: explain which box becomes the containing block for a fixed descendant when an ancestor is transformed
questions.practice: explaining a transformed ancestor as a containing block
questions.stem: A page has a header that is positioned relative to the viewport, and a dialog that applies a transform to animate itself. While the dialog is open, the dialog contains a menu that is positioned fixed with an offset of twenty units from the top and thirty from the left. The dialog's border box begins at three hundred and one hundred and fifty in the page. Where does the menu land, and what is the general rule?

options.text: At thirty and twenty, because a fixed element is always placed against the viewport however the document is built
options.misconception: believes fixed placement ignores the ancestor chain

options.text: At three hundred and one hundred and fifty, because the offsets are zero on the menu and the transform does not change where the containing block begins
options.misconception: believes the containing block is the same box but the offsets are discarded

options.text: At three hundred and thirty and one hundred and seventy, because the transformed ancestor becomes the containing block for fixed descendants, and the same is true of a filter, a perspective, a backdrop filter and a containment value
At the header's position, because a positioned ancestor higher up the tree takes precedence over a transformed one
options.misconception: believes a positioned ancestor wins over a transformed ancestor

questions.explanation: A fixed element is placed against the viewport only when nothing between it and the viewport creates a containing block for it. A transform is on the list of properties that does create one, along with a filter, a perspective, a backdrop filter, a containment value that restricts layout, and a declared future transform, and each of them is listed for the same reason: the engine has to composite the element, and compositing needs a box to composite into. The transform also opens a stacking context, which is why the animation that fixes the containing block is the animation that breaks the menu's placement, and the two failures arrive together. The arithmetic is the ordinary one: the containing block's origin is three hundred and one hundred and fifty and the offsets are twenty and thirty, so the menu lands at three hundred and thirty and one hundred and seventy. The last option is the rule people get wrong by analogy with positioned ancestors, where the nearest one does win; the difference is that a transform creates a containing block for fixed descendants even though it is not itself a positioned value.
questions.hint: Ask what creates a containing block for a fixed element, and then add the offsets to that box's origin.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Where an absolutely placed box with no offsets sits
questions.learningObjective: explain the placement of an absolutely positioned box whose offsets are all at their initial value
questions.practice: explaining the static position of an out-of-flow box
questions.stem: A paragraph is taken out of the flow with an absolute position and no offsets, and its nearest positioned ancestor is a container. The program prints which value each offset computes to and then reports where the paragraph appears. What does it report, and what happens when one offset is given?

options.text: Each offset computes to zero, so the paragraph sits at the container's origin, and giving one offset leaves the other at zero
options.misconception: believes an unset offset behaves as a zero offset

options.text: Each offset computes to its initial value, and the paragraph is placed where it would have been in the flow; giving one offset moves it from that point on that axis only and leaves the other axis at the flow position
Each offset computes to its initial value, and the paragraph is placed at the container's origin because an out-of-flow box has no flow position to fall back to
options.misconception: believes removing a box from the flow also removes its hypothetical position

options.text: Each offset computes to its initial value, and the paragraph stays where it would have been even after an offset is given, because the static position wins over any offset
options.misconception: believes a given offset is ignored for an out-of-flow box

questions.explanation: The initial value of an offset is the word that means no offset was specified, and it is not the same as zero. When every offset is at that value the box has no position to be placed at, so it falls back to the position it would have occupied in the flow, which is why an absolutely positioned paragraph with no offsets usually appears to be in the right place and only its effect on the other content is missing. Supplying one offset breaks the symmetry: that axis is now placed by the offset, measured from the containing block, while the other axis still has no offset and keeps its flow position. The second option is the mistake that makes an unpositioned absolute element jump to the corner of its container, and it is worth knowing the difference because the two values look interchangeable in a reset. The third option is wrong on the point that the hypothetical position is exactly what makes the fallback possible, and the fourth is wrong because a supplied offset is the whole reason the property exists.
questions.hint: Ask what the initial value of an offset is, and whether it is the same as zero.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Which edge an out-of-flow box's offsets are measured from
questions.learningObjective: identify the box that supplies the origin for an absolutely positioned descendant's offsets
questions.stem: A container is positioned relative, has a border of ten and padding of twenty on the top and left, and begins at the origin of the page. An absolutely positioned child of it declares offsets of zero on the top and left and a width of one hundred. Where does the child's box begin, where does the container's visible content begin, and what does that gap tell you?

options.text: The child begins at ten and ten, which is the border edge of the container, and the content begins at thirty and thirty, so an offset of zero places the child over the container's border and padding
The child begins at thirty and thirty, which is where the content starts, and the border and padding are outside the containing block
options.misconception: believes offsets are measured from the inner content edge

options.text: The child begins at zero and zero, which is the page origin, because an absolute box is placed against the page unless the ancestor is the root
options.misconception: believes a relative ancestor does not establish the placement origin

options.text: The child begins at ten and ten and the content begins at ten and ten, so the border and padding do not move the content
options.misconception: believes padding does not push the content in from the border

questions.explanation: Offsets on an out-of-flow box are measured from the padding edge of its containing block, which is the outside of the padding and therefore just inside the border. The container's border is ten, so the origin of the padding edge is ten from the container's own border edge, and a child with offsets of zero lands there. The container's own content starts a further twenty in, because that is what the padding is for, so the content begins at thirty and the child overlaps the ten units of border and the twenty units of padding above and to the left of it. That overlap is the practical point: it is why a dropdown positioned at zero over a padded button appears to sit partly over the button's own edge, and why the usual fix is to offset the child by the padding rather than to try to make the offsets measure from the content. The second option is the misconception the padding edge exists to correct, and the fourth gets the arithmetic wrong twice over.
questions.hint: The origin is one edge in from the border and one edge out from the content; add the border to reach the first and add the padding as well to reach the second.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: What a float changes about the boxes around it
questions.learningObjective: explain the three things taking a box out of the flow with a float changes
questions.stem: An image is given a float to the left and a size. The text that follows it in the source wraps around it, and the box after the text is taller than the image. What changes as a result of the float, and what does not?

options.text: The image leaves the normal flow and is removed from the accessibility tree, so a screen reader no longer reaches it
options.misconception: believes taking a box out of the visual flow removes it from the accessibility tree

options.text: The image stays in the normal flow and the following boxes shift across, so the document's height still accounts for the image
options.misconception: believes a float keeps its place in the vertical flow

options.text: The image leaves the normal flow and the document's height accounts for it as if it were in the flow, so no clearing is ever needed
options.misconception: believes a float still contributes its height to the parent's height

options.text: The image leaves the normal flow so following text wraps beside it and following boxes span the full width; the document's height, the image's place in the accessibility tree, and its place in the tab order do not change

questions.explanation: A float changes exactly three things and leaves everything else alone. It leaves the normal flow, so the boxes after it are no longer shortened and the document's height ignores it, which is why a parent whose only content is a float collapses and why a clearing value is needed to stop the next box from sliding up beside it. It shifts to the side it names, so inline content in the following boxes is shortened to the space beside it and wraps into whatever room is left. And the line boxes of the following content are shifted, which is why a paragraph's first line starts lower than the float's top. What does not change is the order of the boxes in the document, so the accessibility tree and the tab order still see the image in its source position. The second option is the confusion that matters most in practice, because a float is a visual placement and the source order is the semantic one, and any technique that hides content from assistive technology on the grounds that it has been moved out of flow is wrong.
questions.hint: List the effects on layout and the effects on document order separately, and note which of the three effects on layout is the reason clearing exists.
