questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: How far a clearing box is pushed down
questions.learningObjective: compute the offset a clearing box receives from the floats above it
questions.stem: Two floats sit above a block: one floated left whose bottom edge is ninety units from the top, and one floated right whose bottom edge is one hundred and forty. The block itself would start at the top. Four variants of the block are laid out, one for each clearing value, and the program prints how far down each is pushed. What does it print, in the order none, left, right, both?

options.text: Zero, one hundred and forty, ninety, and one hundred and forty
options.misconception: believes the left value consults the right float and the right value the left one

options.text: Ninety, ninety, one hundred and forty, and one hundred and forty
options.misconception: believes even the no-clearing value is pushed down by the float above it

options.text: Zero, ninety, one hundred and forty, and one hundred and forty
Zero, ninety, one hundred and forty, and two hundred and thirty
options.misconception: believes the both value adds the two bottoms together

questions.explanation: A clearing value says which side's floats the box must get past, and the answer is the lowest bottom edge among those floats, expressed as how far down the box has to move from where it would have been. With no clearing the box is not pushed at all, which is zero and is what the layout looked like before floats were introduced. Clearing on the left consults only the left float, whose bottom is ninety, so the box moves ninety. Clearing on the right consults only the right float, whose bottom is one hundred and forty. Clearing on both consults every float and takes the lowest, which here is again the right float at one hundred and forty, and the two are added only if they were stacked vertically rather than beside each other. The fourth option is the arithmetic mistake the geometry invites, and the second is the mistake about which side a value consults, which is worth being precise about because the two floats in this example have different bottoms and so give different answers.
questions.hint: For each value, take the lowest bottom among the floats on the sides it names and subtract the box's own start.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: What an overflow value changes beyond cutting off the overflow
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the effect of each overflow value on clipping, scrolling and the formatting context
questions.stem: A box is given each of five overflow values in turn and the program reports three things: whether overflow is clipped, whether a scroll mechanism appears, and whether a new block formatting context is established. What is the pattern across the five values?

options.text: The default clips nothing; hidden, clip, scroll and auto all clip and open a new context, differing only in whether a scrollbar appears
options.misconception: believes the clip value opens a formatting context like the other three

options.text: The default clips nothing and opens no context; hidden, scroll and auto clip and open a new context; clip clips without a scroll mechanism and opens no new context
The default opens a new context without clipping; hidden and clip clip without a scrollbar; scroll and auto clip with one
options.misconception: believes the default value establishes a formatting context

options.text: All five values clip, and the only difference between them is whether a scroll mechanism appears and whether a new context is opened
options.misconception: believes the default value clips the overflow it can see

questions.explanation: The five values split into three groups, and the groups differ on two axes that are easy to conflate. The default value neither clips nor opens a new formatting context, and content simply overflows visibly, which is why an unstyled box lets its children spill out. The three values that both clip and open a new formatting context are the ones that establish a box the layout has to keep inside: hidden, which clips with no scroll mechanism, and scroll and auto, which clip and offer one, the difference between them being whether the mechanism appears always or only when needed. The value that clips without opening a new context is clip, which was introduced precisely to give the clipping of hidden without the side effect, and that side effect is the reason it exists: a new formatting context changes how the children are laid out, so a tooltip that must not disturb its surroundings clips with clip and not with hidden. The second option is the exact confusion that value was added to fix.
questions.hint: Sort the five values by whether they clip and by whether they open a new formatting context, then read the groups off.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Why clearing a minimum size lets a flex item shrink
questions.learningObjective: explain what a minimum size of zero removes from a flex item's ability to shrink
questions.practice: explaining the minimum size of a shrinking item
questions.stem: A row of flex items contains one item whose text has a long unbroken word. The row is narrower than the content wants to be, and the row overflows. The item has no minimum size declared. What is the floor the layout is applying, and what happens when the minimum size is set to zero?

options.text: The floor is the content's own minimum contribution, which is the width of the longest unbreakable run, and setting the minimum to zero removes that floor so the item takes the size the line gives it and the text overflows or is clipped
The floor is zero by default, so the overflow must come from a property other than the minimum size
options.misconception: believes a flex item has no floor unless one is written

options.text: The floor is the item's declared width, so setting the minimum to zero has no effect because the width still applies
options.misconception: believes a declared width is the floor the layout uses

options.text: The floor is the width of the longest word, and setting the minimum to zero makes the word wrap, because a long run has no break opportunities in it
options.misconception: believes clearing the floor introduces break opportunities into an unbreakable run

questions.explanation: A flex item's default minimum size is not zero, it is content-based, and the content-based floor is the largest minimum contribution the item's content can demand, which for a run of text is the width of its longest unbreakable word. That floor is why a single long identifier inside a flex row makes the row overflow even though everything else is flexible: the item is asked to shrink and the layout refuses below the floor. Setting the minimum to zero removes the floor, and then the item does shrink to whatever the line hands it, and the consequence moves rather than disappears. The long word no longer fits inside the item, so it either overflows visibly past the item's edge, is clipped by whatever clips the item, or makes the item scrollable, depending on what else is set. The fourth option is the trap here: clearing the floor gives the layout permission to make the item smaller, it does not give the text somewhere to break, because a run with no break opportunity has none regardless of how narrow its box is.
questions.hint: Ask what the default minimum size of a flex item is, and separately ask what happens to an unbreakable run when its box gets narrower.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: What a floor on a flexible track does to the row it belongs to
questions.learningObjective: compute the resolved width of a floored flexible track and the overflow it causes
questions.stem: A grid container is 1000 wide with two flexible tracks that each have a floor of 600 and a row gap of 20. The program computes the free space, the ideal share each track would get, the width each track actually ends up at, and the total the row occupies. What are the four numbers?

options.text: Free space one thousand, ideal share five hundred, actual width five hundred each, and a row one thousand and twenty wide
options.misconception: believes the floor is not reached when the ideal share is below it

options.text: Free space nine hundred and eighty, ideal share four hundred and ninety, actual width four hundred and ninety each, and a row one thousand wide
options.misconception: believes a floor reduces the track rather than raising it

options.text: Free space nine hundred and sixty, ideal share four hundred and eighty, actual width six hundred each, and a row one thousand two hundred and twenty wide
options.misconception: believes the gap is subtracted once rather than once per gap

options.text: Free space nine hundred and eighty, ideal share four hundred and ninety, actual width six hundred each, and a row one thousand two hundred and twenty wide, so the row overflows its container by two hundred and twenty

questions.explanation: The row has to pay for its gaps before anything else, so with two tracks and one gap of 20 the free space is 1000 minus 20, which is 980, and the ideal share of that between two equal flexible tracks is 490 each. The floor is 600, and since 490 is below it each track is raised to 600 rather than lowered, which is the whole effect of a floor: it is a minimum, not a maximum. Two tracks of 600 plus the one gap come to 1220, so the row is wider than the container by 220 and the grid overflows. That overflow is the item worth noticing, because a floor that is too generous does not produce a narrower track or a smaller font, it produces a row that runs past the edge of its container, and the failure appears as a horizontal scrollbar or as content clipped by an ancestor rather than as anything wrong with the floor. The fourth option is the arithmetic slip, and the second is the misconception that a floor is advisory.
questions.hint: Subtract the gaps first, divide what is left, and compare that share with the floor before deciding the final width.

questions.topic: What sits between two grid tracks
questions.learningObjective: compute the total width the gaps consume for a given track count
questions.practice: computing the width a row gap consumes
questions.stem: A grid has four tracks of 200 each and a row gap of 16, inside a container 1000 wide. The program prints the width the row uses and the width the gap alone accounts for, then repeats with the gap set to zero. What does it print?

options.text: Eight hundred and sixty-four used, of which sixty-four is gap, and eight hundred with the gap at zero, so there are as many gaps as tracks
options.misconception: believes a row of four tracks has four gaps

options.text: Eight hundred and forty-eight used, of which sixty-four is gap, and eight hundred with the gap at zero, so the extra eight came out of the tracks
options.misconception: believes the tracks were narrowed to pay for the gaps

options.text: Eight hundred and forty-eight used, of which forty-eight is gap, and eight hundred with the gap at zero, so the gap is forty-eight of the container
Eight hundred used, of which nothing is gap, and eight hundred with the gap at zero, so the gap has no effect on an explicit grid
options.misconception: believes a gap does not apply to an explicitly sized grid

questions.explanation: A row of tracks has one fewer gap than it has tracks, because a gap is the space between two neighbours and the last track has nothing after it to be separated from. Four tracks therefore carry three gaps, so 3 times 16 is 48, and 4 times 200 is 800, giving 848 of the 1000 available and 152 left over. Setting the gap to zero drops the row to exactly 800, which confirms that the tracks themselves were not resized: an explicit track size is a size, and the gap is added beside it rather than taken out of it. That is the difference between a gap and a margin on the tracks, which is the third option's confusion. A margin would eat into the space available to the tracks, and a margin between two tracks is not reduced to the larger of the two, so two margins of 16 produce 32 of separation where a single gap of 16 produces 16. The count of one fewer gap is the whole arithmetic here, and it is the number people get wrong most often when a row of many tracks comes out wider than expected.
questions.hint: Count the gaps as one fewer than the tracks, and note that the track sizes are not changed by the gap.

questions.topic: What a cross-axis alignment value decides about an item's size
questions.learningObjective: compare the cross size each alignment value gives a flex item with no size of its own
questions.stem: A flex row is 200 tall on its cross axis and one item has no size of its own and 60 of content. The row is laid out four times, once for each of the alignment values that behave differently here. The program prints the item's cross size and its offset from the start of the cross axis in each case. What does it print?

options.text: Sixty and zero for all four, because an alignment value only moves an item and never resizes it
options.misconception: believes alignment values never affect an item's size

options.text: Two hundred and zero, sixty and zero, sixty and seventy, and sixty and one hundred and forty
Two hundred and zero, sixty and zero, sixty and one hundred and forty, and sixty and zero
options.misconception: believes centring and end alignment produce the same offset

options.text: Two hundred and zero, two hundred and zero, two hundred and seventy, and two hundred and one hundred and forty
options.misconception: believes every alignment value stretches the item first

questions.explanation: The first alignment value is the one that resizes: an item with no cross size of its own is stretched to fill the line's cross size, so it becomes 200 tall and sits at offset zero because it fills the whole axis. The other three move the item without resizing it, so the item keeps its 60 of content height and the remaining 140 is distributed according to the value: none at the start, half of it at each end when centred so 70, and all of it at the end when the value names the end of the axis. The second option is the misconception that makes the value invisible: alignment is not only about placement, and the stretching case is the one a developer relies on when a row of cards is meant to be equal height, so a value written that does not stretch leaves the cards at their content height. The third option confuses centring with the end value, and the fourth applies the stretching rule to values that do not stretch.
questions.hint: Ask whether the value resizes the item or only places it, then subtract the item's own size from the free space to get the offset.

questions.topic: Where a free-space value puts the first item in a row
questions.learningObjective: compute the offset each free-space distribution value gives the first item
questions.stem: A flex row is 1000 wide and holds three items of 200 each, so 400 is free. The row is laid out once for each of five distribution values, and the program prints the offsets of the four gaps, meaning the space before the first item, the two between, and the space after the last. What does it print for the values that pack to the start, centre, distribute between, distribute around each, and distribute evenly?

options.text: Zero; two hundred; zero, two hundred, two hundred, zero; about sixty-seven, about one hundred and thirty-three, about one hundred and thirty-three, about sixty-seven; one hundred four times
Zero; two hundred; zero, four hundred, four hundred, zero; one hundred, two hundred, two hundred, one hundred; about eighty, about one hundred and sixty, about one hundred and sixty, about eighty
options.misconception: believes the free space is split between the items rather than into the gaps

options.text: Two hundred; zero; four hundred, four hundred, four hundred, four hundred; zero, two hundred, two hundred, zero; one hundred, one hundred, one hundred, one hundred
options.misconception: believes centring puts everything at the start

options.text: Zero; one hundred; zero, two hundred, two hundred, zero; zero, two hundred, two hundred, zero; zero, two hundred, two hundred, zero
options.misconception: believes the three distribution values are equivalent

Packing to the start leaves all of it at the end, so the reported offsets are zero. Centring splits it evenly between the two ends, giving 200 at each. Distributing between puts everything in the inner gaps, so the ends are zero and each inner gap is 400 over two, which is 200. Distributing around each item divides the free space by the item count first, giving about 133 per item, and each end then gets half of one of those, about 67, so the ends are smaller than the inner gaps. Distributing evenly divides by the number of gaps rather than the number of items, which here is four because there are three items, so all four are 100 and no end gap is half of anything. questions.topic: What a content condition tests and what it cannot know
questions.learningObjective: distinguish what a content condition measures from the things it deliberately ignores
questions.stem: A rule is wrapped in a condition that requires a viewport of at least 600 wide, and another requires a hovering-capable pointer. The stylesheet author wants one layout for wide screens and a different one for touch. What does each condition measure, and what can neither of them tell the author?

options.text: The first measures the screen the monitor reports and the second measures the screen's pixel density, and between them they identify the device class
options.misconception: believes a width condition reads the physical display rather than the viewport

options.text: The first measures the available width after the browser's own interface is subtracted, and the second measures the number of simultaneous touch points, so a condition is a device query
options.misconception: believes the condition excludes browser interface from the measurement

options.text: The first measures the viewport and the second measures the primary pointer, and between them they tell the author the user's preferred text size and colour scheme
options.misconception: believes a width and a pointer condition also report user preferences

options.text: The first measures the viewport the document is being rendered in and the second measures whether the primary input can hover, and neither can tell whether the layout fits, whether the user has zoomed, or what the device is

questions.explanation: Both conditions are statements about the environment the document is being rendered in and neither is a statement about the device or the user. The width condition reads the viewport, which is the space the document has, not the screen the monitor happens to be, and the difference matters most on a desktop where the window is narrower than the panel. The hover condition reads whether the primary input can hover at all, which is a property of the pointing device rather than of the display, and a touch device with an attached mouse reports a different answer from the same device without one. What neither condition can report is the most important thing a designer wants to know, which is whether the layout fits. That is why a fluid layout with a content-based breakpoint is usually a better answer than a width threshold, because the width that matters is the width at which the content stops working, and that number is a property of the content rather than of the device classes the thresholds are meant to stand in for.
questions.hint: Ask whether each condition reads the space, the input device, or the output device, and then ask which of those the layout actually depends on.

questions.practice: diagnosing a stacking order on an unpositioned box
questions.stem: A card declares a stacking order of 999 and a banner above it declares a position of relative and a stacking order of 1. The card paints underneath the banner, and the card's computed value for the stacking order reads 999 in the inspector. Nothing else about the two elements differs. What is the cause, and what is the smallest change?

options.text: The banner's order of one is smaller, so the card is painted first because the smaller order wins
options.misconception: believes a smaller stacking order paints on top

options.text: The card's order of 999 exceeds the largest permitted value and is clamped, so the two are equal and the earlier one wins
options.misconception: believes a stacking order has a maximum

options.text: The card is unpositioned, so its stacking order is computed and stored but never consulted and it opens no context; give the card a position other than the default
The card is a positioned descendant of a different stacking context, so its order is confined and the comparison never happens
options.misconception: believes an ancestor relationship is what makes an order inert

questions.explanation: The inspector value is what makes this confusing and it is the clue: the declaration is accepted and the computed value really is 999, because the property is valid on any element and the engine stores what it was told. What it does not do is consult it. The order is only read for elements that are positioned or that are items of a flex or grid container, and a static element with no order paints as an ordinary in-flow box regardless of what it says. The banner is positioned, so it opens a context and is placed with the group of positioned descendants, and an ordinary in-flow box is painted before that group, which is the same place its order would have put it. The smallest change is to give the card a position other than the default, or to make it a flex or grid item, and the order will then be honoured. The fourth option is a real mechanism that produces the same symptom, and it is worth checking for as well, but the item's evidence points at the first because there is no intervening context named.
questions.hint: Ask whether the element is one of the kinds whose order the engine actually reads, and check what the property's computed value tells you about the declaration itself.

A developer wraps the rule in a condition requiring a hovering-capable input and the symptom goes away, while the effect still works on a laptop. What does each of those two facts tell you about the mechanism?

options.text: The tap produces a click event that the rule is catching, and the condition changed which event the rule listens for
options.misconception: believes a condition can rebind a rule to a different event

options.text: The tap produces a hover state that the touch device has no way to clear, and the condition excludes the whole rule on the device that cannot hover, so the effect is removed there rather than broken
The description was always visible on the phone and the tap only brought it to the front, and the condition hides it deliberately
options.misconception: believes the state was already applied and the fix was to suppress it

options.text: The card was missing a position, so the hover rule had no effect and the tap revealed it by coincidence
options.misconception: believes the symptom was a stacking or position problem

questions.explanation: A touch screen can produce a hover state, because the first tap of a finger on an element does establish it, and it has no way to end it, because there is no pointer to move away. That is why the state persists after the finger lifts and after a tap elsewhere: the only event that would clear it is the pointer leaving, and there is no pointer. The condition the developer added excludes the entire rule on a device whose primary input cannot hover, so the reveal never happens there at all rather than happening and sticking, which is the right outcome for content that needs a deliberate action to be revealed. What the fix is not is a rebinding: a condition decides whether a rule is part of the cascade, not which event it listens for, and it applies to every declaration in the block rather than to one interaction. The pattern generalises to any effect that depends on a pointer leaving, which is most of the reveal-on-hover family.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Why a feature guard with no fallback leaves the page half styled
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a guard whose failure path was never written
questions.stem: A stylesheet wraps a display and a gap in a condition that tests for a layout feature, and then declares a plain block display and a padding outside the guard. On an engine without the feature the guard's block is discarded entirely, so the display falls back to the outside block, the padding still applies, and the gap is set nowhere at all. What is wrong with the pattern, and what is the smallest change?

options.text: The guard has only a success path, so a discarded block takes its declarations with it rather than falling back to them; the outside block has to carry the values that must hold either way, and the guarded block overrides them
The guard is discarded because the condition names a property and a value rather than a property alone, so nothing inside it applies on any engine
options.misconception: believes a guard naming a value is never supported

options.text: The outside block is applied after the guarded one because it is later in the sheet, so the fallback always wins
options.misconception: believes the outside block is evaluated after the guarded block

options.text: The gap is set to its initial value rather than to nothing, so the failure is a smaller gap rather than a missing one
options.misconception: believes a property inside a discarded block is set to its initial value

questions.explanation: A guard does not merge two blocks or prefer one of them. It is a single rule in the cascade that is either present or absent, and when it is absent the declarations inside it are simply not in the cascade at all, which is why the gap in this case is set nowhere rather than set to a default. The pattern that works is the reverse arrangement: declare outside the guard everything that has to hold when the feature is missing, and put only the override inside it. Then the outside declarations always apply, the guarded ones apply when the engine understands them, and a caller who sees the wrong result knows immediately which side of the guard they are on. The second option is a real restriction and not the one at issue here, since a condition naming a property and a value is the ordinary form. The fourth option is the misconception that makes the failure hard to read in the inspector, where a property that no rule sets looks identical to one set to its initial value.
questions.hint: Ask whether the guarded declarations are in the cascade on an engine that fails the condition, and then ask where the values that must always hold are written.

questions.topic: Why a universal reset has to be overridden everywhere it applies
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a layout whose padding is being removed by a universal rule

questions.stem: A stylesheet opens with a rule that zeroes the margin and padding of every element and switches the sizing rule. A component stylesheet, loaded later, sets a padding of 24 on a card class and a margin on a paragraph. On a page where both stylesheets load, the card has no padding and the paragraph has no margin, and the developer cannot see why. What is happening, and what is the smallest change?

options.text: The universal rule is discarded because a universal selector is not a valid selector, so the card's padding is being removed by something else
options.misconception: believes a universal selector is invalid and ignored

options.text: The component stylesheet loads after the reset and should therefore win, so the failure means the component rule never loaded
options.misconception: believes sheet order alone decides between rules of different scores

options.text: The padding is applied and then removed by the sizing rule the reset switched on, because the sizing rule also clears padding
options.misconception: believes the sizing rule has an effect on padding

options.text: The universal rule scores zero, zero, zero and cannot be beaten by a single class, so it removes the padding from every element including the card; keep the reset and set the card's padding with a selector that outranks it

questions.explanation: The reset wins because of how the three columns are compared, not because of when it was written. A universal selector contributes nothing to any column, so the reset scores zero, zero, zero, and a class selector scores zero, one, zero, which is higher in the second column and therefore wins no matter which stylesheet it came from. That is the whole point of a reset and also its cost: it applies to every element, so every component that wants a margin or a padding has to outrank it, and a single class is not enough. The second option is wrong because a universal selector is perfectly valid, and the third is the mistake that makes this hard to diagnose, since the instinct is to look at the load order when the score is what decided. The fourth option confuses two properties, and the sizing rule has nothing to do with padding. The two reasonable repairs are to set the component's padding with a selector that outranks the reset, or to scope the reset so it does not reach the component's elements at all.
questions.hint: Score the reset's selector and the component's selector, and compare the columns rather than the sheet order.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Why a dialog that animates with a transform captures a fixed header
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a fixed element that scrolls with the page once a transform is introduced above it
questions.practice: diagnosing a transformed ancestor capturing a fixed box
questions.stem: A page has a header that stays put while the document scrolls. A modal dialog is animated by applying a transform to the dialog's wrapper for the duration of the animation, and the wrapper is an ancestor of the header's containing block. The symptom is that the header scrolls with the page for as long as the dialog is open and settles back afterwards. What is the cause, and what fixes it without giving up the animation?

options.text: The transform is applied to the wrapper's parent, so the header's containing block is unchanged and the symptom must come from the dialog's own stacking order
options.misconception: believes only a direct parent can become a containing block

options.text: The header loses its position because the transform resets it, so the fix is to re-declare the position after the dialog opens
options.misconception: believes a transform on an ancestor clears a descendant's own position

options.text: The transform makes the wrapper a containing block for fixed descendants, so the header is placed against the wrapper rather than the viewport; animate an opacity or a size property instead, or apply the transform to an inner layer only
The header is fine and the dialog's wrapper is scrolling, so the fix is to stop the wrapper from scrolling rather than to change the animation
options.misconception: believes the symptom is a scrolling container rather than a containing block

questions.explanation: A transform does two things, and only one of them is usually expected. It opens a stacking context, which is why the dialog reliably covers the page, and it becomes the containing block for any fixed descendant, which is why the header stops being fixed. The containing block is found by walking up, and a transform counts even though it is not a positioned value, so the wrapper is chosen and the header's offsets are measured against it. That wrapper then moves with the animation, and the header moves with the wrapper, which is exactly the observed behaviour: the header scrolls for the length of the animation and settles when the transform is removed. The fix follows from the two effects being separable. Animating an opacity or a size changes the appearance without creating a containing block, and if the transform has to stay for the effect, applying it to a layer inside the dialog rather than to a wrapper above the header leaves the header's ancestor chain untouched. The third option is the belief that a transform on an ancestor rewrites a descendant's own properties, which it does not do.
questions.hint: Ask which ancestor a fixed element finds as its containing block, and list the properties that can create one without being a position.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Why a floored track pushes a row past the width of its container
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a grid row that overflows because a track floor is too generous
questions.practice: diagnosing a grid row that overflows its container
questions.stem: A grid container is 1000 wide and its two columns are each written as a flexible track with a floor of 600 and a column gap of 20. The layout is correct on a wide screen and produces a horizontal scrollbar on a narrow one, with the content cut off at the right edge. The developer did not change the floor. What is happening, and which two figures explain it?

options.text: The gap is being added twice, once as a gap and once as the space the floor reserves, so the row is 1000 plus 440; removing the gap fixes it
options.misconception: believes the floor reserves space in addition to the gap

options.text: The free space is 980, the ideal share is 490, and the floor raises each track to 600, so the row is 1220 wide and overflows by 220; lower the floor or let one track be the flexible one
The tracks are being sized before the container's width is known, so the floor is applied against a provisional width and never revised; forcing a reflow after load fixes it
options.misconception: believes track sizing uses a width that is later corrected

options.text: The floor is being applied to the gap rather than to the tracks, so the row's gap has grown to 600; setting the gap explicitly fixes it
options.misconception: believes a floor can land on the gap

questions.explanation: The arithmetic is the whole diagnosis. The row pays for its one gap first, leaving 980 to share, which would be 490 per track if the floors did not intervene. The floor of 600 is above that share, so both tracks are raised to it, and 1220 plus the gap is a row wider than the 1000 available, which is the scrollbar. Nothing about the floor is wrong in itself: on the wide screen the share clears 600 and the floors never engage, which is why the layout looks correct there and only fails when the container narrows. That is the general shape of a floor-based layout failure, in that the condition that triggers it is a width nobody tested. The two repairs are to lower the floor to something the narrowest supported container can accommodate, or to make one track the flexible one and give the other a fixed width, so that the flexible track absorbs the shortfall instead of both tracks refusing to give ground. The second option invents a mechanism, and the fourth is a category error, since a floor applies to a track and not to the gap between tracks.
questions.hint: Compute the free space after the gap, the share each track would get, and then what the floor does to that share.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Why a marked override outlives the thing it was meant to escape
questions.learningObjective: diagnose an override that has become the strongest declaration in the sheet
questions.practice: diagnosing an override that outranks everything
questions.stem: A utility class sets a padding with importance so that it beats a component's padding. A year later a new component rule with a much stronger selector still cannot change the padding of an element carrying the utility, and the developer adds a second marked rule with a stronger selector still. The stylesheet now has four marked declarations of the same property. What has gone wrong, and what is the durable arrangement?

options.text: Each marked rule outranks every normal rule in the origin, so the newest one wins by being the only marked one, and the component can never win without marking as well; put the component's padding in a later layer and drop the marking
Only the first marked rule counts and the later ones are ignored, so the padding has been fixed since the utility was written and the component's problem is its score
options.misconception: believes an important declaration is honoured only once per property

options.text: The marks are cancelled by the presence of a stronger selector anywhere in the sheet, so the last marked rule has already been neutralised
options.misconception: believes a stronger normal selector cancels importance

options.text: The padding is set four times and the result is the sum, so the element's padding is larger than any single rule asked for
options.misconception: believes repeated declarations of a property accumulate

questions.explanation: Importance is checked before the score, so among the declarations that set this property only the marked ones are in the contest, and the score comparison among them is the only tiebreak. The newest marked rule wins, which is why the developer's second attempt appeared to work, and the component can never win without marking too, so the sheet is now in an arms race it can only lose. The durable arrangement uses the mechanism designed for exactly this case: a layer is compared before the score but after importance, so putting the component's rule in a layer declared after the utility's layer wins on the layer comparison without needing to mark anything, and any future component can do the same. The marks then come out, and the sheet has one place where the override relationship is written down instead of being distributed across four declarations. The first option is the only one of the four that describes the mechanism accurately, and the third is the belief that would make a developer conclude the opposite of what happens.
questions.hint: Ask how many declarations survive the importance check, and what the first comparison among the survivors is.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Why a relative selector written the wrong way round matches nothing
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a rule that selects a parent by looking forward for something that is above it
questions.practice: diagnosing a relative selector with the wrong direction
questions.stem: A stylesheet holds a rule that styles an element by testing whether it is followed by a later sibling, and a second rule that tests whether a container has a particular kind of child. The second rule is written against the child and tests for its own wrapper, and it never applies. The first rule, written the other way round against the container, applies correctly. What is wrong with the second rule?

options.text: The rule is valid but scores too low to beat the component stylesheet, so it never applies even where it matches
options.misconception: believes a rule that matches can still be dropped for scoring low

options.text: The rule is dropped because a relative selector may not be used on a class selector that names the subject element
options.misconception: believes the argument of a relative selector cannot be a class

options.text: The rule is applied and then overridden by a later rule for the same element, so it never shows
options.misconception: believes a matching rule is always overridden when another exists

options.text: A relative selector only looks forward, from the element being tested towards its descendants and the siblings that follow it, so a child cannot test for an ancestor; write the rule against the wrapper instead

questions.explanation: The direction is fixed and it is the only thing that makes the first rule work. A relative selector is evaluated from the element being tested: the argument is looked for inside that element's own subtree, or among the siblings that come after it, and never among its ancestors or the siblings before it. A child therefore cannot ask whether it has a wrapper, because the wrapper is behind it in the tree, and the rule is not merely low-scoring or overridden, it never matches anything, which is why there is no sign of it at all rather than a sign of it losing. Writing the rule against the wrapper and putting the descendant in the argument reverses the direction and matches, which is what the first rule in the item does. The two ways to express that are to test for the descendant from the container, or to test for the immediately following sibling from the thing that precedes it, and the second form only works for an adjacent sibling. The general habit is to write the test from the element you want to style, which is the only element the selector can be attached to.
questions.hint: Ask, for the element being tested, whether the thing named in the argument is inside it or after it, and never behind it.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Counting what a descendant selector reaches and scoring it
questions.learningObjective: count the elements a descendant selector matches and score the selector
questions.practice: counting matched elements and scoring a selector
questions.stem: A document has a wrapper carrying a class, containing a list carrying another class, containing three list items. A resolver matches five selectors against the three items and reports how many items each one reaches. The five are a last-child form under the list, an adjacent-sibling form under the list, a descendant form naming the wrapper and the list, a form naming an identifier, and a second-child form. First give the number of items each form reaches, then give the specificity of each, and say what the counts tell you about the cost of the widest of them.

options.text: Three, three, three, none and one item respectively, with the same scores, so the sibling forms are as broad as the descendant form
options.misconception: believes a sibling form reaches every item in the list

options.text: Three, two, one, none and three item respectively, with the same scores, so the last-child form is the broadest of the five
options.misconception: believes a positional form matches every position

options.text: One, two, three, none and one item respectively, with scores of zero, two, one; zero, one, two; zero, two, one; one, zero, one; and zero, two, one, so the descendant form has to be tested against every item in the list
One, two, three, none and one item respectively, with the descendant form scoring zero, two, two because the list contributes a second type column
options.misconception: believes the wrapper and the list are both type selectors

questions.explanation: The three items are siblings inside the list, and that relationship is what decides all five counts. A last-child form reaches only the item in the last position, so one. An adjacent-sibling form reaches each item that has an item after it, so the first two and not the third, which is two. A descendant form naming the wrapper and the list reaches all three. A form naming an identifier that appears nowhere reaches none, which is the cheapest result and the first thing to check when a rule appears to do nothing at all. A second-child form reaches the item in the second position, so one. The scores follow from the two columns each form spends: the last-child, descendant and second-child forms each name a class and a type selector, so they score zero, two, one; the sibling form names two type selectors and one class, so it scores zero, one, two; and the identifier form scores one, zero, one, which is the highest of the five and still matches nothing, which is the sharpest illustration in the item that a score says nothing about whether a selector matches. The cost point follows from the counts: the descendant form is tested against every element in the document, so its cost scales with the tree rather than with the list it names.
questions.hint: Establish the sibling relationships first, then count how many items each form reaches and score the parts each one names.

questions.topic: The free space in a row of three items and the offset under each alignment
questions.learningObjective: compute the free space in a flex line and the offset each alignment gives the first item
questions.practice: computing free space and alignment offsets
questions.stem: A flex line is 1000 wide and holds three items of 200, 200 and 300. First give the free space, then give the offset the first item receives under each of five alignment values, and say which of the five changes the size of an item rather than only its position.

options.text: Two hundred and fifty free, then offsets of zero, one hundred, zero then one hundred then zero, one hundred at the ends with one hundred between, and fifty four times, and the centring value changes the size of an item
options.misconception: believes every value divides the free space by the item count

options.text: Three hundred free, then offsets of zero, one hundred and fifty at the ends, zero then one hundred and fifty then zero between, fifty at the ends with one hundred between, and seventy-five four times, and none of the five changes an item size

Three hundred free, then offsets of zero, one hundred and fifty, zero then three hundred then zero, three hundred at the ends with three hundred between, and seventy-five four times, and none of the five changes an item size
options.misconception: believes the around and evenly values put all the free space into the inner gaps

options.text: Three hundred free, then offsets of zero, one hundred and fifty, zero then one hundred then zero, zero at the ends with two hundred between, and fifty four times, and the between value changes the size of an item
options.misconception: believes a distribution value resizes an item rather than distributing space

questions.explanation: The free space is 1000 less the 700 the three items occupy, which is 300, and every offset follows from dividing that 300 according to the value. Packing to the start leaves the first item at offset zero. Centring splits the 300 between the two ends, so 150 before the first item. Distributing between puts it all into the two inner gaps, so the first item is still at zero and each inner gap is 300 over two, which is 150. Distributing around each item divides the free space by the item count first, giving 100 per item, and halves one of those at each end, so 50 before the first item and 100 between neighbours, which is why the ends of that value are thinner than its inner gaps. Distributing evenly divides by the number of gaps rather than the number of items, which here is four because there are three items, so all four are 75. The last half of the question separates the axis families: these five all work along the main axis and none of them resizes anything. The value that resizes belongs to the cross axis, and the one that does so is the stretching value, which affects only an item with no size of its own on that axis. Confusing the two families is what produces a row whose items are a different size from the one that was set.
questions.hint: Subtract the item widths from the line, then work out how many gaps the value creates before dividing.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: How many tracks a repeating template creates and how many rows the items make
questions.learningObjective: compute the track count a repeating template produces and the row count for a given number of items
questions.stem: A grid container is 500 wide and its template repeats a track with a floor of 120 and a maximum of one fraction, separated by a gap of 20. First give the number of tracks the repeat produces, then say what happens to a run of eight items in terms of rows, and then say what changes if there are only two items and the value is the fitting variant rather than the filling one.

options.text: Three tracks, because three floors and two gaps fit in 500 while four do not, so eight items make three rows of three, three and two, and the fitting variant collapses the one empty track leaving two
Four tracks, because four floors and three gaps fit in 500, so eight items make two rows of four and the fitting variant has nothing to collapse
options.misconception: believes the gap count is ignored when fitting the tracks

options.text: Three tracks, so eight items make three rows of three, three and two, and the fitting variant leaves the empty track in place because it only changes how tracks are sized
options.misconception: believes the fitting variant resizes rather than collapses

options.text: Three tracks, so eight items make two rows of four and two, and the fitting variant collapses two empty tracks
options.misconception: believes the items can use more tracks than were created

questions.explanation: The track count is the largest number of tracks whose floors and gaps together fit, so the arithmetic is floors times count plus gaps times one less than the count. Three floors of 120 with two gaps of 20 is 400, which fits in 500, and four floors with three gaps is 540, which does not, so three tracks are created and the remaining 100 is shared out as extra width on top of each floor. Eight items in three tracks fill the first row, fill the second, and put the remaining two in the third, so three rows. The fitting variant is the interesting part and it is the one developers get wrong: it does not change how the tracks are sized, it collapses the tracks that have no item in them, so with two items the third track is collapsed to zero and the two items take the whole width. That is the difference between the two variants in one sentence, and it is the reason a fitting template gives a row of two cards at full width while a filling one gives two cards and an empty third of the same width.
questions.hint: Fit as many floors and gaps as will fit, then compare the item count with the track count for the row count and the collapsing behaviour.

questions.topic: Which conditions a narrow viewport satisfies and how many there are

questions.stem: Six conditions are written: a minimum width of 600, a maximum width of 600, a range form that requires at least 600, a range form that requires under 600, a hovering-capable input, and a coarse pointer. The environment is a viewport 360 wide and 640 tall with no hovering input and a coarse pointer. First say which of the six hold, then give the count, then say what the two that are almost the same actually differ in.

options.text: The minimum-width one, the maximum-width one, the hovering one and the coarse-pointer one hold, so four of six, and the first and third are different tests with different results
options.misconception: believes a narrow viewport satisfies a minimum-width condition

options.text: The maximum-width one and the hovering one hold, so two of six, and the range form is a different test from the prefixed form
options.misconception: believes a coarse pointer excludes a hovering condition

options.text: All six hold, so six of six, and the range form is a different test from the prefixed form
options.misconception: believes a condition list is an or over its members rather than six separate tests

options.text: The maximum-width one, the under-600 range one and the coarse-pointer one hold, so three of six, and the first and third are different spellings of the same test rather than different conditions

A viewport of 360 fails a minimum of 600 and passes a maximum of 600, the range form that requires at least 600 fails for the same reason the prefixed minimum fails, and the range form that requires under 600 passes for the same reason the prefixed maximum passes. A touch device with no hovering input fails the hovering condition and passes the coarse-pointer condition, giving three passes out of six. options.misconception: believes a row of three columns carries three gaps

options.text: One hundred and eighty each, two gaps totalling sixty, summing to 600, and with a width of two hundred the count is three with each column one hundred and eighty

options.misconception: believes covering and filling are the same for a picture wider than its box

options.text: Filling draws it at about two thirds, covering at one, and containing at about two thirds, so the same scale serves the last two
options.misconception: believes filling and containing pick the same scale

questions.explanation: The scale is the ratio the picture is drawn at, and each of the three values takes a different one of the two ratios the pair of sizes offers. Filling ignores both ratios and uses one, so the picture is drawn at 400 by 300 inside a 400 by 200 box and simply overflows vertically. Covering takes the larger of the two ratios, so it compares 400 over 400, which is one, against 200 over 300, which is about two thirds, and takes one; the picture is therefore drawn at its natural 400 by 300 and the excess 100 of height is cut off, half at the top and half at the bottom because the cut is centred. Containing takes the smaller ratio, which is the two thirds, so the picture is drawn at about 267 by 200 and the spare width of about 133 is split into about 67 on each side. The point worth keeping is that the natural ratio of one and three quarters to one never changes under covering or containing, because only the scale changes, and that is what distinguishes these two from a box that crops the picture to a different shape on purpose.
questions.hint: Take the two ratios, then pick the larger for covering and the smaller for containing; the cut is centred so the excess splits in half.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Why a later layer beats a more specific rule
questions.learningObjective: explain why raising a selector's score cannot win against a later layer
questions.stem: An application's stylesheet needs to override a component library's button padding. A developer first tries a more specific selector, then a longer one, then an important declaration, and only then discovers layers. Explain why the first three attempts are unsatisfactory, what the layer comparison changes, and what the four attempts say about the design.

answer.exemplar: A selector's score is a liability that persists after the declaration it was written for has been settled. Choosing a more specific selector to beat the library's rule does resolve today's conflict, but it changes the shape of the sheet permanently: the winner now carries a higher score than the property ever needed, and the next person who needs a different value for that same property has to outrank the winner rather than outrank the library. Every such attempt adds another rung, and the sheet becomes a ladder in which each rung is only meaningful relative to the one below it. That is a cost paid by everyone who touches the file afterwards, including people who never intended to change the button, and it grows without any single decision looking wrong. Writing a longer selector is the same move made more slowly, with more selectors to read and no change to the underlying problem. Importance avoids the ladder but pays in a different currency. An important declaration is consulted before the score, so it wins, and it also wins over every normal declaration written after it. The developer who later needs to fix the problem the first override created finds that their own careful rule is ignored, because the tool they reached for is still holding the property. So the override is not merely in the wrong place, it is in a place nobody can reach, and the failure is invisible until someone looks at the computed value. Layers are different in kind rather than in degree, and the difference is which comparison is consulted. With layers, the two declarations are compared by their layer ranks before the engine looks at a score at all, so a rule in a later layer wins on that first comparison and its own selector never enters the argument. A developer can therefore override the library with a selector as plain as the library's own, which means the two rules can be read side by side and understood without arithmetic. The layer order is where the override relationship is written down, once, in a form a person can read at the top of a file, and it works the same way for a declaration written today and for one written next year by someone who has never seen this one. The four attempts in sequence also describe the underlying design fault. Each of them is a reasonable response to a sheet that offers no way to say this declaration is meant to win over that one, so the absence of a layer is not a missing feature but a missing place to put an intention. Adopting layers is not free: the order has to be declared before any of the participating sheets use it, so the sheets have to agree on a shared order, and a library that wants to be overridable has to put its own rules in layers and document which ones it intends to be escaped. That is a real coordination cost, paid once, and it replaces a per-override cost paid by every future change.

questions.explanation: A model answer has to make three separate arguments: that a score is a standing cost, that importance wins in a way nobody can later override, and that a layer changes which comparison is consulted rather than raising the score. Answering only that a later layer wins is not enough, because the item is about why the first three attempts were unsatisfactory rather than about what the fourth one does.
questions.hint: For each of the three failed attempts, ask who pays the cost later, and then ask which comparison the fourth attempt actually changes.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Why a negative stacking order can make a child invisible
questions.learningObjective: explain why a negative stacking order paints behind the background of its own container
questions.practice: explaining a negative stacking order against a background
questions.stem: A card has an opaque background, opens a stacking context, and contains a decorative layer given a negative stacking order. The layer is in the markup and has a size, and it cannot be seen. A developer raises the order to a large positive number and the layer appears but now covers the card's text. Explain what is happening, and describe the two arrangements that produce the intended result.

answer.exemplar: The painting sequence inside a stacking context is fixed, and the first thing it paints is the background and borders of the element that forms the context. Only after that does it paint the child contexts that carry negative orders, and only after them the in-flow content, then the floats, then the inline content, then the positioned descendants, and finally the children with positive orders. A negative order is therefore not a way of being slightly behind the siblings; it is a way of being behind the container's own background, because the background is painted first of all. The card is the element that forms the context, its background is opaque, and the decorative layer with a negative order is painted after that background and so is hidden by it. This is the reason the technique is used in one direction and not the other: a negative order on a child of an element with a transparent background is visible, because there is no opaque background to cover it, and that is how a watermark that sits behind a transparent panel is built. Raising the order to a large positive number is the wrong repair rather than a slow one, and the reason is the position of that step in the sequence. A positive order paints after the in-flow content, which is where the card's text is, so the layer now covers the text instead of the background. The two arrangements that work both change which step of the sequence the background is painted in rather than moving the layer. The first is to take the background off the card and put it on an element that does not form the context, or on a context of its own ordered below the layer, so that the layer's negative order puts it above that background and still below the text. The second is to give the layer its own stacking context with a positive order, so the whole group sorts into the positioned-descendant step, after the text, and then place the text into its own context with a higher order so the text is painted last. Both arrangements are a little more markup and a little more reasoning than the one declaration that started it, and that is the general shape of this area: the order is a statement about a fixed sequence, so anything that looks like a small ordering tweak is usually a small structural change.

questions.explanation: A model answer has to place the negative order and the background in the same fixed painting sequence and show that the background comes first, then give two repairs that change where the background sits rather than how large the order is. Recommending a large positive order misses the item, because that is the second symptom in the stem and the reason it is wrong.
questions.hint: Write out the painting sequence for a stacking context from the background onwards and locate both the background and the layer in it.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Why a percentage padding follows the container rather than the element
questions.learningObjective: explain why a percentage on a box follows its container and what that makes fluid
questions.practice: explaining the reference box for a percentage length
questions.stem: A card declares a padding of five percent, and a developer expects the padding to be five percent of the card's own width. At one viewport the two happen to agree and at another they differ by a factor of two, and the gutters grow as the window widens. Explain which box a percentage padding is taken against, why the padding on the inline and block axes both use it, and what property of the result makes it useful and what makes it surprising.

answer.exemplar: The reference box for a percentage padding is the containing block, and specifically its inline size, which is the horizontal dimension in a horizontal writing mode. It is not the element's own width, and the distinction is easy to miss precisely because the two coincide whenever the element fills its container, which is the common case in a simple layout. The factor of two in the second observation follows from the element being half the width of its container: the padding is computed as a share of the wider box and then applied to the narrower one, so the padding ends up a tenth of the element's width rather than a twentieth. Both axes use the inline size, and that is worth understanding rather than memorising. A percentage of the block size would need a percentage of a height, and a height is very often not known at the time the padding is resolved, since it is usually the result of the content and of the padding itself, so the specification uses the one dimension that is reliably available. The consequence is that vertical padding scales with the width, so a card that becomes shorter does not get shorter gutters, and a card in a landscape phone gets proportionally thinner vertical gutters than the same card in a portrait one. Both of those are correct under the rule and both surprise people. The property that makes the result useful is that it keeps proportion. A card whose padding is a share of its container keeps the relationship between its gutter and its content as the layout reflows, so a fluid grid of cards does not develop heavy borders at wide viewports and hairline borders at narrow ones, and a design that intends a fixed gutter has to say so with a length rather than a percentage. The property that makes it surprising is the same thing seen from the other side: a card that occupies only part of a wide container picks up a padding sized for the whole container, so a narrow sidebar inside a wide row carries a gutter that looks out of proportion to the sidebar, and the only remedies are a length, a custom property, or a container whose width tracks the card rather than the row.

questions.explanation: A model answer has to name the containing block and the inline size, say why the block size is not used even for the block-axis padding, and then give both the benefit and the trap. Stopping at the containing block is not enough, because the item asks why the vertical padding behaves the way it does too.
questions.hint: Ask which dimension of which box is reliably known when the padding is resolved, and then check what the two agree-on cases have in common.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Why a rule outside every layer beats the whole layered system
questions.learningObjective: explain the unlayered tier and the reason the specification put it above every layer
questions.practice: explaining the unlayered tier of the cascade
questions.stem: A design system ships three layers and documents that an application may override them. An application rule written outside any layer beats every layered rule, and the design system's documentation asks for it to be layered as well. Explain the rule that puts the unlayered tier at the top, what the tier is for, and what changes when the application's rule is put in a layer of its own.

answer.exemplar: The rule is positional. The engine ranks a declaration outside any layer above every declaration inside a named one, and it does so before the score is consulted, so an unlayered rule wins on the first comparison that separates it from any layered competitor. A sheet that must override a whole layered system can therefore do it with one ordinary declaration written as plainly as the system's own, and the system's specificity is irrelevant. The tier exists for exactly that case, and it is the design's escape hatch rather than an oversight: without it, the only way out of a layered system would be importance, which outranks every later normal rule and is therefore a tool that cannot be aimed at one property in one place. The unlayered tier is aimed. It beats the system, it does not beat the future, and it is visible in the source as a rule with no layer name, which a reader can recognise. The design system's request that the application's rule also be layered is a request about maintainability rather than about the outcome. Putting the rule in a layer declared after the system's last layer reaches the same winner, because the layer comparison is what decides it either way, and it costs one statement at the top of the sheet. What changes is where the decision lives. Outside every layer, the override is decided by the tier and cannot be reordered by anyone. Inside a layer, the override is decided by the layer order, and that order is a shared artefact: the system and the application both have to agree on it, so the order has to be declared somewhere both can see, and a sheet that joins later has to know which position it is claiming. That is a real cost, and it is the cost the design system is asking the application to accept, because the benefit is that the override becomes part of a described arrangement instead of a privileged exception. The failure mode of not layering is easy to describe: a project accumulates unlayered overrides, each one working, none of them ordered relative to each other, and two of them touching the same property are then decided by score alone, which is the situation the layers were introduced to remove. So the tier is the right default for a one-off emergency override and the wrong default for a project's standing relationship with a system.

questions.explanation: A model answer has to place the unlayered tier in the order of comparisons, say what the tier is for, and then explain the difference between the two arrangements in terms of where the decision lives rather than in terms of the winner. Saying both arrangements win is half the item.
questions.hint: Ask which comparison decides the outcome in each arrangement, and then ask who can change that comparison afterwards.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Ordering the checks that decide one declaration's value
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps the engine takes to decide which declaration wins for a property
questions.stem: A property is set by five declarations: one in an earlier layer, one in a later layer, one unlayered, one with importance inside a layer, and one with importance outside every layer, all on the same element and all with different selectors. Put these five checks in the order the engine makes them, naming the check that the last two declarations between them pass and the check that decides the outcome if the two important ones are in the same layer.

options.text: Compare the importance of the declarations, so that the two marked ones are the only ones left, and drop everything normal
Compare the layer ranks, reading the order in reverse for the important group and with a declaration outside every layer ranked lowest among important ones
Compare the scores, from the identifier column through the class column to the type column, and stop at the first column that differs
Compare the sheet order of whatever declarations are still tied, and the earliest one in the sheet wins
Declare the layer order, so that the position of each layer is fixed before any rule is compared, which is a setup step rather than a comparison

questions.explanation: The order exists because each step discards declarations, and a discarded declaration never enters any later comparison, which is why the sequence rather than the set of checks is the thing to remember. The layer order is a setup step, not a check, and it comes first because the two checks that follow it need the ranks it fixes. Importance is checked next and it is the most destructive of the checks, because it removes every normal declaration in the same origin regardless of how specific any of them is, which is exactly what the two marked declarations in this question rely on. The layer ranks come third, and the reversal for the important group is part of that step rather than a step of its own, so a marked declaration in an earlier layer beats one in a later layer while the opposite holds for normal ones. The score comparison comes fourth and is the first check these five declarations reach that is the familiar one; it is also the check that would decide the outcome if the two marked declarations were in the same layer, in which case the layer comparison separates nothing and the score column by column does the work. The sheet order is last and is only consulted when every earlier check has tied, so the option that claims the earliest declaration wins is wrong by construction.
questions.hint: Ask at each step how many declarations are still in the contest, and remember that one step is a setup rather than a check.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Ordering the painting steps inside one stacking context
questions.learningObjective: sequence the painting steps that decide which sibling appears on top
questions.stem: One element opens a stacking context and has children of several kinds: a child with a negative order, an in-flow block, a float, an inline run, a positioned child with no order, a child with a reduced opacity, and a positioned child with a positive order. Put these seven steps in the order the engine paints them, naming the step that covers the two children which opened contexts without an order.

options.text: Paint the child contexts with positive orders, from the smallest upwards, so a larger positive order is painted later and appears on top
Paint the background and borders of the element that forms the context
Paint the in-flow, non-positioned block descendants, then the floats, then the inline content
Paint the positioned descendants and the children that opened a context with no order, together in tree order, which is where the positioned child with no order and the reduced-opacity child both go
Paint the child contexts with negative orders, from the most negative upwards

questions.explanation: The sequence is a property of the platform rather than of the document, and two of its features cause most of the confusion. The first is that the context's own background is painted before anything else, which is why a negative order can put a child behind it, and the second is that the three middle groups are painted in a fixed order in which in-flow content comes before floats and floats come before inline content, so a float sits above the blocks that follow it and inline text sits above both. The fourth step is the one people misremember, because a positioned child with no order and a child that opened a context through a property such as a reduced opacity go in the same step, in tree order, rather than in separate steps. That grouping is the answer to the named part of the question and it is why a reduced-opacity element cannot be positioned above a positioned sibling without a real order. The last step sorts the positive orders from the smallest upwards, which is counter-intuitive to anyone expecting the largest to be painted first, and it is the reason a larger positive order appears on top.
questions.hint: Start with the context's own background, then work through the negative, in-flow, float, inline, unordered and positive groups in that order.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Ordering the steps that turn a written width into a used width
questions.learningObjective: sequence the resolutions a width passes through before a box is painted
questions.stem: A box declares a width, a padding and a border, sits inside a container, and a grid or flex rule may also apply to it. Put these five resolutions in the order the engine performs them, naming the step at which a percentage width is resolved and the step at which the outer width becomes available to the parent layout.

options.text: Resolve the declared width to a used width, turning a percentage into a length against the containing block and evaluating any length functions
Apply the sizing rule, adding the padding and border to the content width under the initial rule or taking them out of it under the alternative one
Run the layout of the parent, in which the box's outer width occupies space and any automatic size on the other axis is settled from the content
Substitute any custom properties and inherited values, so that the declaration is complete before it is compared
Read the cascade for the box and settle which declaration of the width applies, using the layer, score and sheet-order checks in turn

questions.explanation: The order matters because two of these steps change what a later step is comparing, and getting it wrong produces answers that look plausible and are wrong. Substitution comes first, since a declaration that refers to a custom property or to an inherited value is not complete until those are read, and comparing incomplete declarations would give a score for a value nobody will use. The cascade comes next, and it decides which of the competing declarations of the width is the one being resolved, which is the step the whole of the layer and score discussion sits inside. Resolution of the declared value into a used value follows, and this is where a percentage is turned into a length against the containing block and where the length functions are evaluated, so a width written as a minimum of a percentage and a length is a single number by the end of this step rather than an expression the layout has to understand. The sizing rule is applied after that, and it is the step that decides whether the padding and the border sit outside the declared number or come out of it, which is why the two rules must be applied to a resolved length rather than to a percentage. The parent's layout is last, and it is the step at which the outer width finally exists as a quantity the parent can place against, which is also where a height that was left automatic is settled from the content.
questions.hint: Ask which step makes a declaration complete enough to compare, and which step is the first one that needs a number rather than an expression.

questions.subject: WEB_DEVELOPMENT
questions.topic: Ordering the checks that decide whether a selector matches one element
questions.learningObjective: sequence the parts of a selector that a matcher checks from right to left
questions.stem: A selector has a type part, a class part, an attribute test and a positional pseudo-class, and it is matched against every element in a document. A matcher logs the checks it performs. Put these five steps in the order a right-to-left matcher performs them, naming the step whose failure lets the matcher discard the element immediately and the step that is repeated for each ancestor as it walks up.

options.text: If there is no combinator left, the selector matches; otherwise the next compound to check has already been read and the walk continues
Confirm the element is a candidate at all, so that text nodes and other non-element nodes are discarded before any selector is tested against them
Check the compound selector at the right-hand end against the element, testing the class, the attribute and the positional pseudo-class against the element's own state and siblings
Read the combinator that joins this compound to the one before it, which says whether the next candidate is a parent, an immediate child, or a following sibling
Move to the candidate the combinator named, and repeat the compound check against it, which is the step that runs once per level of the ancestor chain

questions.explanation: The order is right to left because the right-hand end is the only part of the selector that names the element actually being tested, and everything to its left is a condition on that element's context. The cheap filter comes first, since a text node between two elements can never be the subject of a selector and is discarded before any work is done on it. The compound at the right-hand end is checked next, and a failure here is the answer to the named part of the question: the element is discarded immediately, with no walk up the tree at all, which is why a selector that starts with something the element does not carry is cheap even when the rest of it is long. The combinator is read to learn what kind of candidate the next compound belongs to, and the step that repeats per ancestor is moving to that candidate and running the same compound check against it, because each level has its own class, attribute and positional tests. The last step is the base case of the recursion, and it is the point at which a match or a non-match is decided. The practical consequence for anyone writing selectors is that putting the specific, cheap-to-fail part on the right and the broad part on the left is what makes a selector fast, and the reverse habit is why a sheet with one deeply nested selector can be slow on a large document.
questions.hint: Start with the cheapest check that can discard the element, and ask what the matcher does after the right-hand compound succeeds.
